# Bollywood blockbuster KUCH KUCH HOTA HAI to celebrate 30th anniversary Edinburgh International Film Festival

![Rachel Fergusson](https://www.thestar.co.uk/jpim-static/image/2025/09/12/9/57/RachelFergusson.jpg?width=96&crop=1:1,smart)

Live Reporter

## The 90s rom-com was partly filmed in Scotland and will return to the cinema in 2028 for its 30th anniversary

The Bollywood cult favourite film KUCH KUCH HOTA HAI will celebrate its 30th anniversary at the [Edinburgh International Film Festival](/arts-and-culture/edinburgh-festivals/edinburghs-festivals-2026-here-are-all-the-festivals-taking-place-in-the-capital-this-august-and-whats-happening-at-them-8837788 "Edinburgh's Festivals 2026: Here are all the festivals taking place in the Capital this August - and what's happening at them") (EIFF).

The festival, which runs every year in August, announced the landmark film will return to the big screen in Edinburgh as part of its 2028 edition.

## Sign up to our daily newsletter

### Thank you for signing up!

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to Edinburgh News, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Partly filmed in Scotland, the return will celebrate the rom-com’s enduring legacy in Indian cinema, with director Karan Johar and other guests in attendance.

[From breaking news at Holyrood to what’s on this weekend – get Edinburgh’s news, sport and lifestyle stories in our daily newsletter](https://www.edinburghnews.scotsman.com/newsletter)

Karan Johar was invited to mark KUCH KUCH HOTA HAI’s 30th anniversary at the EIFF in 2028 during a meeting he hosted in the Mumbai offices of his production company, Dharma Productions, earlier this week with the [First Minister John Swinney](/news/edinburgh-council-to-ask-john-swinney-to-close-loophole-on-short-term-let-licensing-9320064 "Edinburgh council to ask John Swinney to close loophole on short-term let licensing") and Screen Scotland’s Interim Executive Director David Smith.

![Iconic Bollywood film KUCH KUCH HOTA HAI was partly filmed in Scotland](https://www.edinburghnews.scotsman.com/jpim-static/image/2026/10/30/10/42/unnamed-(43).jpg?trim=0,87,0,0&width=640&quality=65)
![placeholder image](/img/placeholder.jpg)

The meeting focused on Scotland’s potential as a destination and partner for Indian film and television production.

KUCH KUCH HOTA HAI was the first major Indian production to film extensively across Scotland, including Eilean Donan Castle, Glen Coe, Tantallon Castle and Inchmahome Priory.

Scottish landscapes are an important part of the film’s visual identity, and established a lasting connection between Scottish landscapes and Indian popular cinema.

[First Minister John Swinney](/news/edinburgh-council-to-ask-john-swinney-to-close-loophole-on-short-term-let-licensing-9320064 "Edinburgh council to ask John Swinney to close loophole on short-term let licensing") said: “It was a pleasure to meet Karan Johar in Mumbai, and I am delighted that he has accepted the Edinburgh International Film Festival’s invitation to celebrate the 30th anniversary of KUCH KUCH KOTA HAI which holds a special place in the hearts of communities across Scotland and beyond.

“I look forward to welcoming him to Edinburgh. During my visit to India, I met with people from the Indian film industry, including representatives from Dharma Productions, to discuss opportunities for future collaboration between Scottish and Indian filmmaking.

“Scotland’s screen industry has tremendous potential as a creative partner for Indian film and television, offering the infrastructure, expertise and world-class filming locations to support a wide range of productions.”

EIFF CEO andFestival Director Paul Ridd said: “At EIFF we are always thinking about the future and what’s next.

“So we jumped at an opportunity like this, to plant the seeds for a celebration of a legendary, much-loved film at our Festival, a film featuring Scotland and some of the most iconic stars of Bollywood cinema on screen.

“We can’t wait for what promises to be something truly special for our 81st edition in 2028. But in the meantime, watch this space for more news of our 80th next August.”

Further details on the 2027 Festival will be announced in the coming months.

# Long Rise of Sourdough

### Three bakers, three ovens, one smell drifting from their doorways before the rest of us are even up

SRQ Magazine | November 2026

By Sarah Emily Miano

In [Restaurants](/articles/category/Restaurants)

# Photo 2

![Photo 2](/clients/52/assets/c52_articles/20261027130929346.jpg "Photo 2")

# The Bakero

By sunrise, bakers across Sarasota have been awake for hours.They’ve worked the dough, checked their starters, silenced one timer after another. Three hours in, the deck ovens throw enough heat for the first batch. Steam rolls out when the doors open, and the aroma of fresh bread fills the bakery. M.F.K. Fisher, the influential American food writer, called that smell “indescribable in its evocation of innocence and delight.” Loaves emerge golden brown, ticking as they cool. Before commercial yeast appeared in the nineteenth century, bread began with flour and water left to ferment; wild yeasts and naturally occurring bacteria made it rise. Egyptians baked like this around 1500 BC. Gold Rush miners helped make sourdough a San Francisco habit. In 2010, Chad Robertson’s Tartine Bread handed the artisan bread movement a blueprint: natural leaven, barely handled dough, long fermentation. The ideal loaf emerged with a crackling crust and an open, custardy crumb. Sixteen years later, people want sourdough more than ever. The bakers that local folks ask for by name are making it in small batches, by hand, because they can’t help themselves.

Owner and head baker of the newly opened The Bakero, Natalia Lugowska, learned her craft in Warsaw before moving to Sarasota in 2024 with her family. Years of experience taught her that “it’s difficult to have everything under control.” A proof answers to any number of things, not to a clock, so she adjusts her morning to whatever the dough is doing. “Sometimes it’s ready today faster than yesterday, so you need to react,” she says. 

The most important factor: all-organic flour, she says, which keeps out glyphosate, a.k.a Roundup, which Florida testing found in most supermarket loaves. She settled on Central Milling Company in Utah. Her fermentation takes three or four warm hours, then some nineteen in the cold. “The gluten develops for so long. It helps the bread to be very easy to digest,” she explains. High hydration and steam off the oven’s hot stone crisp the crust without hardening it. “It’s very similar to how our grandmas were making bread in a stone oven.” Slice a loaf and the crumb webs into pockets. Bite the heel for crunch, then take the long chew. It’s the lightest of the three breads here, great for tearing, though it toasts up beautifully, too.

The Main Street cafe offers a classic white, a whole-wheat, a five-seed of sunflower, pumpkin, flax, sesame and poppy, a baguette with a crisp golden shell and a bread of the week. Order the Bakero Plate and the sourdough becomes the centerpiece of breakfast: whipped European butter, an organic soft-boiled egg with a runny yolk, aged gruyère, half an avocado, a scatter of flaky salt, plus ham or smoked salmon. It’s continental-style breakfast at its best, and a clear expression of Lugowska’s vision: simple quality ingredients, prepared carefully, with bread at the forefront. 

The bakery opens at half past six and closes at two. Lugowska starts at four or five and finishes when the doors do. “The most important thing for me is to have a nap after work, and then I recover and continue my day,” she says—a baker’s schedule summarized in one sentence.

# 

**![Photo 3](/clients/52/assets/c52_articles/20261027130929980.jpg "Photo 3")**

![Photo 3](/clients/52/assets/c52_articles/20261027130929980.jpg "Photo 3")

# **Bread Bandits**

You have likely eaten the bonny loaves of Bread Bandits, since they supply the St. Regis, Indigenous, Pura Vida and other kitchens around town. Jules Thuet is a sixth-generation baker in his family. “The first part happened over a hundred years ago,” he says. His father moved from France to Canada, toting the family starter, out of Alsace, which is more than a century old. Jules brought it south. “I smuggled it down here. To keep it alive. Much like wine, our sourdough, it’s like a terroir.” His business partner, Brad Rutledge, came up through the Thuet family bakery and rose to head baker, then took the same post at Blackbird in Canada. Jules made the pitch: “These people, they want good bread. Let’s bring it to them.” So Rutledge packed up his life, too. Bread Bandits uses Bagatelle flour from Moulins Foricher, an independent family mill that strictly sources and grinds its grains in the Loire Valley. Thuet likes it because, as he puts it, this terroir produces high-quality, sustainable wheat certified under French CRC standards, and that character shows up in the loaf with a creamy flavor and soft, open interior. Filtered water, sea salt, flour, starter. Zero yeast, a point Thuet makes passionately. “Tons of people say, this is sourdough bread, and then you look at the ingredients, and it has yeast,” he says. “In France, they would put you in prison for that.” 

The dough ferments for thirty to forty-six hours. “People started introducing machines, and these profit-driven methods, which sped up the process,” Thuet says, sacrificing the time needed for the bread to predigest itself. “That’s what sourdough does. It’s breaking down a lot of the things naturally, and turns into a completely different product. It’s easy to digest and also has tons of beneficial nutrients.” The menu shows hydration figures like a wine list shows vintages: multigrain, seventy-one percent; rye, sixty-nine. Baguettes are seventy-three percent, the backbone of the popular Tuna Bandit sandwich with tarragon aioli and crispy onions. “We filter our water of all chlorine and PFAS [per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or “forever chemicals”]. But the natural minerals left that we have in our Sarasota water make incredible bread,” Thuet says. “The NYC water myth has gone too far! Great bread can be made on the Gulf Coast. Crediting water for people’s bread would be the same as crediting the ball for a Messi goal.”

Specials rotate daily: cranberry walnut, challah, potato cheddar, olive-rosemary. There are even sourdough croutons. The multigrain is Thuet’s own pick, thanks in part to twelve hours of toasting before the grains ever meet dough. “Other loaves, they’re just throwing birdseed in there. There’s no flavor added, and it actually soaks up a lot of water. Whereas ours has a beautiful, nutty, toasted flavor.” Every slice feels indulgent as much as virtuous, so you go back for another whether you care about fiber or not. Walk into Bread Bandits on South Osprey seven days, or visit the Venice and Lakewood Ranch markets. A second location recently opened in Lakewood Ranch, with a pastry test kitchen, so they can expand their offerings.

# 

![Photo 4](/clients/52/assets/c52_articles/20261027130929263.jpg "Photo 4")

![Photo 4](/clients/52/assets/c52_articles/20261027130929263.jpg "Photo 4")

# Camelot Breads

Down on Swift Road, in a plaza you would drive past a gazillion times without braking, Michael Toporowski of Camelot Breads works behind a two-century-old dough trough he found in a small town in Provence. The owners declined to sell.  
“As long as you take out enough money, things can happen,” he says. Fifty loaves’ worth of dough can rise in that wooden hull at a go, then two people can lift it by the handles and flip the mass onto the table. “This is the way they used to do it,” he says. A flaxseed linen cloth, also a callback of hundreds of years, covers the dough without sticking.

Toporowski came to this late, with intention. “I retired from banking at 55, sat around for a couple of months, my golf wasn’t very good, so I decided to go back to school and got a culinary degree,” he says. He wanted to see how commercial kitchens operated, and to learn the correct methods for safety and scaling up. Every year since, he has taken a class from another master baker. “Here I am, an old student. But you find your passion, you find your dream, and that’s where you go.”

Bread here starts with the mill. In the front room sits a stone flour mill, made in Ukraine on the German pattern, crickety and loud as it works. Stone grinding treats the grain gently and keeps its nutrition intact; the mill handles fifty pounds in half an hour and sifts to any grade from fine to coarse. Ancient grains—spelt, einkorn, kamut, sprouted Red Fife—come from Central Milling. Rye berries arrive from Jack Melton’s family farm near Dade City. “We try to incorporate all the grains,” he says, handfeeding the hopper while flour spills out below.

Today’s starter comes up white, glossy and bubbling, fully alive and ready to work. With digestion in mind, he aims for a total acidity near four, and fermentation lasts twenty-six to forty-eight hours. “We want the bread to be fermented enough that when you eat it, the digestive process has already started enough.” Hand-mixing the dough, he talks structure. “Flour has a disulfide bond,” he says. “The gluten structure when it forms is long and stringy, so if we use a mixer, we’re going to break that bond. That’s similar to taking a pane of glass and shattering it, and then trying to put it back together. You’ll have a bunch of little pieces.” The stretch-and-fold method keeps the network intact, opens more surface to the yeast and bacteria and evens the temperature through the mass. The dough holds enough water that the loaves go straight into baskets afterward. Leave them on the counter and gravity interferes. 

Camelot’s miche follows Poilâne’s lead, one massive country round (3kg, 9 to 10 lbs) that he portions into quarters, its flours—organic wheat, spelt and rye—milled on baking day. Toporowski scores the dough so the wheel won’t tear as it rises. The crust comes up very dark, then gets dusted through stencils so each loaf gets marked with diagonal stripes, wheat fronds or whatever holiday pattern is apt. The miche eats like a robust table bread, dense and husky with a mild sourness that stands up to stew, yet never heavy. It also makes a terrific ham-and-cheese—or croque-monsieur, if you will. 

Multigrain—wheat and millet to flax and barley—comes out with a nubbier crumb, gently tangy. Toporowski bakes a shelf of ryes, one with sauerkraut. There’s an epi scored so it tears apart into rolls. “Little buns ready to go,” he says. The focaccia emerges with whole rosemary sprigs, sea salt and good olive oil, a masterpiece he insists anyone can manage at home. “You just get it in your hands, and you want to play the piano to stretch it out.”

Nothing leaves Swift Road for a supermarket or restaurant. Saturdays, Camelot sets up at the Sarasota Farmers Market; Sundays in Lakewood Ranch. Miss both, you wait a week. And yet people do wait. In season, the line wraps around the block, and Camelot produces 1,000 to 1,200 loaves a week. For a baker working this way, the demand tells you plenty. “There aren’t many people doing this sort of thing around town,” he adds.

Long fermentation does what these bakers claim. Phytic acid breaks down so more iron and zinc reach you; bacteria consume the carbohydrates that cause bloating; blood-sugar climbs more gently after a meal. Most supermarket sourdough skips that process entirely. Commercial yeast manages the rising in an hour or two, and vinegar or citric acid fakes the tang. One taste reveals the difference. **SRQ**

# Sourdough starter is full of live bacteria, so why isn’t sourdough bread considered a probiotic food?

By [Ryan Brennan](/profile/315990134/) Trend Hunter

If you’ve ever kept a sourdough starter on your counter, you know it has a personality. It bubbles, it rises and it gets hungry if you forget about it for a few days.

That’s because a [sourdough starter is very much alive](https://trendhunter.com/trending/cards/the-science-of-sourdough-bread-how-fermentation-shapes-your-loaf?utm_source=mcc&utm_medium=iacontcard&utm_campaign=thtest&utm_content=top&cid=cmt_con_iacta-top_mcc-thtest). It’s packed with wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria that feed on flour and ferment it over time.

So it seems logical to assume the loaf that comes out of the oven is alive, too. After all, bacteria and yeast are the same things that make foods like yogurt, kefir and kimchi popular for gut health, and it’s the probiotics, which the [National Institutes of Health](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Probiotics-Consumer/) describes as live microorganisms found in some fermented foods, that do the bulk of that work.

Which raises the obvious question: Does sourdough bread have probiotics? The short answer is no, and it comes down to one thing: heat.

[Harvard’s Nutrition Source](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/probiotics/) notes that heating, baking or pasteurizing fermented foods can kill the live microorganisms that would otherwise make them probiotic. In other words, the yeast and bacteria thriving in your starter don’t survive a trip through a hot oven in any meaningful numbers.

So, no, sourdough isn’t probiotic and won’t deliver healthy bacteria to your gut. But that doesn’t mean your gut gets nothing out of it.

## Sourdough bread can still feed the good bacteria already in your gut

Here’s the good news. Sourdough bread may not be probiotic, but it does offer prebiotics, and those matter, too.

“Sourdough bread ferments over time. That’s what causes those bubbles to form and creates holes in the bread when you cut into it,” registered dietitian **Beth Czerwony** told [Cleveland Clinic](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/benefits-of-sourdough-bread). “Fermentation creates prebiotics, which are what feed the healthy bacteria in your gut.”

During that long fermentation period, the yeast and bacteria in the starter spend hours breaking down parts of the flour and reshaping the dough. Even though those microbes don’t make it through baking, some of what they leave behind can still benefit the bacteria already living in your gut.

That puts sourdough in a different category from gut-health favorites like yogurt or kefir:

* Probiotic foods provide live microorganisms
* Prebiotic foods help feed the microbes already in your gut

In other words, [prebiotics and probiotics](https://www.star-telegram.com/entertainment/living/article315767541.html) do different jobs, but they’re meant to work together: one supplies the beneficial microbes, while the other helps give those microbes something to feed on.

## Sourdough bread can help your gut in other ways, too

Feeding your gut bacteria isn’t the only perk of that slow fermentation. Because the yeast and bacteria have already spent hours breaking down the flour, your digestive system gets a bit of a head start.

That’s one reason sourdough bread may feel easier on your stomach than some other breads.

**Allison Wells**, a senior instruction specialist in Purdue University’s Department of Food Science, explained in a [Campus Insights Media](https://www.campusinsightsmedia.com/purdue/03631190-63c4-4b2b-b934-6f3f22739fcc/) video that by the time the dough hits the oven, the microorganisms in the starter have already begun breaking down starches and other larger components.

That breakdown can also include some FODMAPs, a group of carbohydrates that are hard for some people to digest and may trigger bloating, gas and other symptoms in people with IBS. According to a [2018 review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6110937/) published in *Nutrients*, the yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough can break down some of those compounds during fermentation, which may be part of the reason some people find it gentler on their stomachs.

Of course, all of that happens in the dough. The bigger question is whether it makes a difference once the bread is actually in your body, and there’s some evidence that it does. A [2019 study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31817104/) in *Nutrients* followed 36 healthy adults and found that sourdough breads moved through parts of the digestive tract faster than bread made with baker’s yeast alone.

Still, “easier to digest” doesn’t mean easier for everyone. The effect depends on the flour, the starter and the fermentation process, and researchers say the human evidence is still mixed.

And no matter how long it ferments, sourdough still contains gluten, so it isn’t a safe option for people with celiac disease.

## How to turn sourdough bread into a synbiotic snack or meal

Sourdough may not bring probiotics to the table on its own, but it plays well with foods that do.

When you pair a prebiotic food with a probiotic one, you’re creating what’s often called a [synbiotic combination](https://www.charlotteobserver.com/living/article315775002.html), giving your gut both the beneficial bacteria and something for them to feed on.

A few easy ideas:

* Sourdough toast with Greek yogurt and berries on the side
* Sourdough topped with cottage cheese that contains live cultures
* Sourdough with a yogurt-based spread and sliced vegetables
* Sourdough alongside kefir and fruit for breakfast
* Sourdough topped with sauerkraut or kimchi that still contains live cultures
* Sourdough with labneh made from yogurt with live active cultures
* Sourdough toast with avocado, plus a small serving of yogurt or kefir

The key is to check the label. Not every fermented food still has live microorganisms by the time it reaches your plate, so look for wording like “live and active cultures.”

So while the idea of a sourdough probiotic doesn’t quite hold up, [sourdough bread](https://trendhunter.com/trending/cards/the-science-of-sourdough-bread-how-fermentation-shapes-your-loaf?utm_source=mcc&utm_medium=iacontcard&utm_campaign=thtest&utm_content=bottom&cid=cmt_con_iacta-bttm_mcc-thtest) still earns a spot in a gut-friendly diet. It just plays a different role, feeding the good bacteria you already have and pairing easily with the foods that bring in more.

# $60 for a loaf of bread? New York bakery has customers lining up

RYE, a popular new bakery in New York opened by Martin Auer, specializes in 100 percent rye sourdough bread. Captured from BuzzFeed Tasty's social media account

By **Jane Han**

* Published
* Updated

NEW YORK — Korea may have its bread pilgrimages, but Manhattan has taken the bakery craze to another level: $60 for a single loaf of rye bread.

RYE by Martin Auer, an Austrian bakery that opened in Manhattan's SoHo neighborhood in September, has quickly become one of the city's most talked-about food destinations, drawing crowds and widespread media attention for its unusually expensive sourdough rye bread.

The 1.5 kilogram loaf costs $60, but customers can also purchase half a loaf for $30 or a quarter for $15.

Located on Lafayette Street, the bakery specializes in just one type of bread. Its minimalist interior looks more like a high-end retail showroom than a traditional bakery, with customers able to watch the bread-making process.

The bread contains just three ingredients: organic rye flour, water and salt. According to the bakery, the dough undergoes a fermentation process lasting up to 24 hours, using a sourdough starter more than 50 years old.

But the price has raised eyebrows, particularly because a comparable loaf from the same bakery sells for roughly $16 in Austria.

The bakery says the higher New York price reflects the cost of importing ingredients from Austria, the labor involved in making the bread and Manhattan's high operating expenses.

The hefty price tag has sparked criticism and jokes on social media, with some questioning whether any bread is worth $60.

The attention, however, has also brought customers through the door. The bakery reported that even though they are new to the scene, the bread sells out on a regular basis, as curious New Yorkers lined up to see what made the loaf so special.

The craze may sound familiar to Koreans, where “ppangji sullye,” or bread pilgrimages, have become popular among bakery enthusiasts willing to travel long distances and wait in line for famous baked goods.

At $60 a loaf, the New York bakery is testing just how much customers are willing to pay for bread.

## Forgotten Trades: Pioneer Skills are Making a Comeback

Pioneer-era skills have made a resurgence among Americans. Things like sourdough baking, sewing, raising chickens, cows, and bees, are gaining popularity with some starting their own full-fledged self-sustaining farms.

![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/4f45ea8d0c7ce55244ef4c5d0861e7b4ca9a987c3bdedc13536b6923574b9e54?s=48&d=mm&r=pg)

by

[Morgan Olsen](https://utahstories.com/author/molsen/)

|

---

When Pioneers began their trek West in the 1800’s, skills such as sewing, food preservation, carpentry, blacksmithing, and water purification were not only important, but necessary to their survival. As modern inventions became available in the decades following, people relied less on those skills over time, and the art of developing those once-crucial skills became viewed as “old-fashioned” by some.

In recent years, however, these Pioneer-era skills have made a resurgence among Americans. Things like sourdough baking, sewing, raising chickens, cows, and bees, are gaining popularity with some starting their own full-fledged self-sustaining farms. Some even post about their off-grid lifestyle on social media and, in doing so, have gained hundreds of thousands of followers.

“As a child, I spent hours reading through my parents’ *The Complete Encyclopedia Of Crafts*, while at the same time, I was totally fascinated by the early PC clone my father bought and I couldn’t get enough of what it could do and how it could do things faster and easier,” said Dan Maker of [Provo Pioneer Village](https://www.provopioneervillage.org/). “I first learned wood working in my father’s shop, and I learned to cook and sew and knit from my mother. I’ve spent 35 years making my living working with computers, and all the while I’ve been learning more hand crafts, spinning and weaving, more woodworking, silversmithing, blacksmithing. I’m always trying to find balance between the two opposites; I’m sure that is part of why interest is increasing in traditional hand crafts.”

While the Internet and rise of social media influencers has seemingly increased the popularity of Pioneer skills, Sue Blazzard, assistant director at the [McQuorie Memorial Pioneer Museum](https://www.dupstgeorge.org/) in St. George, says she thinks the Internet has been a positive change that has helped more people learn these skills even if they weren’t passed down to them by a family member.

“I think Pioneer skills were dying out because we weren’t passing them along like previous generations were,” said Blazzard. “But now, if anyone wants to learn those things, they can find them on the internet and that is a really cool thing. Hopefully, that means the knowledge of these skills will stick around.”

Maker has a similar opinion, pointing out the fact that the rise of the Internet has made it easier for us to have unlimited knowledge at our fingertips.

![](https://utahstories.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/doc09-handcraft-revival-web-IMG_5452.jpeg)

Inside Handcraft Revival.

“Social media, specifically, and the internet in general, have made these skills and their history so much more accessible,” he said. “It used to be that you had to know someone personally that knew how to do something; now you can open Instagram or Twitter, or Youtube on your phone and find a dozen people telling how they are doing or have done what you are interested in.”

Some of these skills include things like growing food, canning, and freeze-drying food. As new information is discovered about processed foods, many are opting for the organic lifestyle to improve their health.

“Planting gardens and farming, even in little pots or on small plots of land, has become very popular,” Blazzard said. “And then people want to preserve the food that they’ve grown so they can have those fresh nutrients, so canning and freeze-drying has also increased in popularity.”

While the Pioneers relied on growing their own food in order to have food to eat, it is a skill that is benefitting people generations later.

Pioneers also relied on quilting, knitting, and crocheting, all of which have seen an uptick in popularity in recent years.

“Quilting has become a big deal,” said Blazzard. “Back in the day, that was what they had to do to make their bedding. And knitting and crocheting was how they made socks to keep their feet warm. They didn’t have much choice but to learn how to do those things.”

Maker agrees that learning these skills is important to a child’s development.

“I think all of the skills the Utah Pioneers had are still relevant today,” said Maker. “At a most basic level, if we understand what they had to do to live, we will be far more appreciative (in most cases) of how much less we must do and how much more we can choose to do, or not do in our day-to-day lives.”

Founded by Jennifer Samuelson and Melissa Mott, [Handcraft Revival](https://handcraftrevival.com/) in Salt Lake City hosts an after school program that teaches these valuable skills to kids today.

“We offer after-school classes in machine sewing, handwork, as well as a seasonal craft club,” said Samuelson. “Each class runs for a 10-week session, giving children enough time to truly learn a new skill, build confidence, and complete a meaningful project from start to finish. Our instructors have years of experience teaching handwork to children and carefully guide students at their own pace. We use beautiful, natural materials like wooden knitting needles, wool yarn, cotton fabric, and other quality supplies because we believe children deserve to work with real tools and materials that are both functional and inspiring.”

These skills have a significance to them that has held up through the past 200 years.

“I think these skills are important for both children and adults because our hands and our brains are deeply connected,” said Samuelson. “Activities that require fine motor skills help develop coordination, dexterity, attention, and problem-solving. They also encourage a pace of life that teaches patience, persistence, and sustained focus. As a teacher, I’ve seen firsthand how handwork can help children settle after a busy school day. There is something that feels deeply regulating about working rhythmically with your hands, and many students leave our after-school class feeling calmer, more confident, and proud of what they’ve created.”

Samuelson and Mott both enjoy teaching the after-school classes and love to see the different ways her students approach different tasks.

“One of my favorite parts of teaching these classes is watching children experience success in ways that aren’t measured by grades or test scores,” said Samuelson. “They discover that they can learn something difficult, overcome mistakes, and create something beautiful and useful with their own hands. That sense of competence and joy stays with them long after the project is finished. I think that’s something we could all use a little more of.”

## Sajal Aly asks fans to choose kindness over hate

![](http://www.magtheweekly.com/assets/uploads/updates/2026-10-21/27756_1794259_updates.jpg)

Sajal Aly shared a message for her fans on how supporting a favourite celebrity should never come at the expense of putting someone else down.

Taking to social media, the actor urged her followers to refrain from spreading hate or negativity in her name, stressing that a fan’s behaviour can also reflect on the person they claim to support. “Being someone’s fan doesn’t mean you have to hate or put down others. In fact, when you claim to represent someone, your words and actions reflect on them too,” Sajal wrote.

She went on to address her fans directly, encouraging them to approach online conversations with kindness rather than hostility. “To all my fans, I hope you always choose love over hate, appreciation over negativity and kindness over aggression. Support the people you love but never at the expense of someone else,” she said.

The actor added a particularly direct message for those who may use her name while attacking others: “If you’re spreading hate in my name, you’re not really my fan.”

# The Habits Guide: How to Build Good Habits and Break Bad Ones

On this page

Before we get into the guide, I want to recommend the most comprehensive guide on how to change your habits and get 1% better every day: My #1 New York Times bestselling book *[Atomic Habits](http://atomichabits.com).*

Packed with evidence-based self-improvement strategies, *Atomic Habits* will teach you how to make the small changes that will transform your habits and deliver remarkable results.

*Atomic Habits* will reshape the way you think about progress and success and give you the tools and strategies you need to transform your habits—whether you are a team looking to win a championship, an organization hoping to redefine an industry, or simply an individual who wishes to quit smoking, lose weight, reduce stress, and achieve success that lasts.

Let’s get to the habits guide…

## What Are Habits?

Let’s define habits. Habits are the small decisions you make and actions you perform every day. According to researchers at Duke University, habits account for about 40 percent of our behaviors on any given day. 

Your life today is essentially the sum of your habits. How in shape or out of shape you are? A result of your habits. How happy or unhappy you are? A result of your habits. How successful or unsuccessful you are? A result of your habits.

What you repeatedly do (i.e. what you spend time thinking about and doing each day) ultimately forms the person you are, the things you believe, and the personality that you portray. Everything I write about – from [procrastination](https://jamesclear.com/procrastination) and [productivity](https://jamesclear.com/productivity) to [strength](https://jamesclear.com/strength-training) and [nutrition](https://jamesclear.com/eat-healthy) – starts with better habits. When you learn to transform your habits, you can transform your life.

## Did you know?

The Origin and Etymology of Habit

The word *habit* most often refers to a usual way of behaving or a tendency that someone has settled into, as in "good eating habits."

In its oldest sense, however, *habit* meant "clothing" and had nothing to do with the things a person does in a regular and repeated way. Today, this meaning is preserved only in phrases like "nun's habit," "monk's habit," and "riding habit" (clothes worn for horseback riding).

Like so many words that appeared in English in the centuries following the Norman Conquest, *habit* came from French. Indeed, the modern French word for clothes is *habits* (pronounced \ah-bee\). In English, *habit* progressed from meaning “clothing” to “clothing for a particular profession or purpose” to “bearing, conduct, behavior." (The word’s evolution brings to mind the old adage “the clothes make the man," which asserts that the way we dress reflects our character.)

From “what one wears” to “how one conducts oneself,” *habit* continued to evolve, referring to appearance (“a man of fleshy habit”) and mental makeup (“a philosophical habit”) before, after several centuries in English, it came to mean repeated activity: “a behavior pattern acquired by frequent repetition.”

The specific development of *habit* to refer to drug addiction began in the 19th century, with reference to opium.

Interestingly, even though “clothing” is the oldest meaning of *habit* in English, it wasn’t the original meaning of the word's ultimate Latin root, *habitus*. In Latin, that word’s original meaning was “state of being” or “condition.”

Our most common use of *habit* today, “acquired mode of behavior,” didn’t exist in Latin—*habitus* went from meaning “condition” to “how one conducts oneself” to “clothing.” That it was adapted into English in precisely the reverse order is an accident of history; the order of meanings absorbed from one language to another rarely constitutes a logical development. As with all language, meaning is established by usage and force of habit.

Choose the Right Synonym for *habit*

[habit](/dictionary/habit), [practice](/dictionary/practice), [usage](/dictionary/usage), [custom](/dictionary/custom), [wont](/dictionary/wont) mean a way of acting fixed through repetition.

[habit](/dictionary/habit) implies a doing unconsciously and often compulsively.

had a *habit* of tapping his fingers

[practice](/dictionary/practice) suggests an act or method followed with regularity and usually through choice.

our *practice* is to honor all major credit cards

[usage](/dictionary/usage) suggests a customary action so generally followed that it has become a social norm.

western-style dress is now common *usage* in international business

[custom](/dictionary/custom) applies to a practice or usage so steadily associated with an individual or group as to have almost the force of unwritten law.

the *custom* of wearing black at funerals

[wont](/dictionary/wont) usually applies to a habitual manner, method, or practice of an individual or group.

as was her *wont*, she slept until noon

her riding *habit*

a nun's *habit*

2

**:** a usual manner of behavior or thinking

his *habit* of taking a morning walk

3

**:** a way of behaving that has become fixed by being repeated often  compare [reflex entry 1 sense 1](/dictionary/reflex?ref=kidsdictionary#kidsdictionary)

4

**:** characteristic way of growing or occurring

elms have a spreading *habit*

## Medical Definition

habit

noun

hab·​it

[ˈhab-ət](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/habit?pronunciation&lang=en_us&dir=h&file=habit001 "How to pronounce habit (audio)")

1

**:** bodily appearance or makeup especially as indicative of one's capacities and condition

a man of fleshy habit

2

**:** a settled tendency or usual manner of behavior

3

a

**:** a behavior pattern acquired by frequent repetition or physiological exposure that shows itself in regularity or increased facility of performance

the daily bowel habit

b

**:** an acquired mode of behavior that has become nearly or completely involuntary

locked the door through force of habit

c

**:** [addiction](/dictionary/addiction#medicalDictionary)

was forced to steal to support his drug habit

4

**:** characteristic mode of growth or occurrence

# Why Habits Can Be a Good Thing

Brown University Health Blog Team

January 23, 2024

![Women exercising at gym]()

We all have habits. They are part of our daily lives. A habit is a repeated action that becomes an automatic behavior, with little to no thought. From getting out of bed and brushing our teeth to what and when we eat, these routine behaviors become part of us.

Some habits are good, others bad. For example, flossing your teeth regularly is good for your health. But if you skip flossing, that’s a bad habit because it can have negative effects on your health.

Whether good or bad, habits are hard to break. You can thank your brain for that. These routine behaviors are formed by a process called habituation. That means your brain gets better at performing a specific action over time.

## How good habits support wellness

While bad habits such as [smoking](https://www.brownhealth.org/be-well/be-quitter-benefits-smoking-cessation-and-how-start-quitting "Be a Quitter! The Benefits of Smoking Cessation and How to Start Quitting") or non-stop [snacking](https://www.brownhealth.org/be-well/healthy-snacks-reach "Healthy Snacks to Reach For") can have a negative impact on you, positive habits can improve your health and well-being. Here’s why habits can be a good thing:

* **Efficiency.** Habits help make us more efficient. That means it requires less thinking and effort for your brain to do that task. [Daily activities](https://www.brownhealth.org/centers-services/alzheimers-disease-memory-disorders-center/daily-rituals-healthy-brain "Daily Rituals for a Healthy Brain ") are easier because they become automatic. That gives your brain more energy for other tasks.
* **Consistency.** Developing positive habits helps promote regularity and stability and leads to a more predictable and stable routine. Regular activities also help us to develop discipline and self-control.
* **Goal Achievement.** Many habits help us achieve long-term goals. If we break down larger goals into smaller, manageable habits, they become more achievable and sustainable over time.
* **Health and Wellness.** Healthy habits, such as [regular exercise](https://www.brownhealth.org/be-well/fresh-start-create-workout-routine-works-you "A Fresh Start: Create a Workout Routine that Works For You"), a [balanced diet](https://www.brownhealth.org/be-well/mediterranean-diet-best-weight-loss-heart-health-and-longer-life "Mediterranean Diet Best for Weight Loss, Heart Health, and Longer Life"), and [sufficient sleep](https://www.brownhealth.org/be-well/get-your-zzzs-sleep-tips-and-how-get-back-track "Get Your Zzzs: Sleep Tips and How to Get Back on Track"), contribute to physical and mental well-being. These habits also lower your risk for various health issues, such as [heart disease](https://www.brownhealth.org/be-well/heart-disease-women-often-different-men "Heart Disease in Women Is Often Different Than In Men"), [stroke](https://www.brownhealth.org/be-well/reduce-your-stroke-risk-live-healthy "Reduce Your Stroke Risk: Live Healthy"), cancer, and [diabetes](https://www.brownhealth.org/be-well/what-diabetes-mellitus "What is Diabetes Mellitus?").
* **Time Management:** Developing habits around time management helps individuals use their time more effectively. Planning and prioritizing can lead to increased productivity and a better [work-life balance](https://www.brownhealth.org/be-well/finding-your-best-work-life-balance "Finding Your Best Work-Life Balance").
* **Stress Reduction:** Knowing what to expect and having structured routines can reduce uncertainty and stress. Habits can create a sense of control and stability in one's life.
* **Skill Development:** Consistent practice is a form of habit that is crucial for skill development. Whether it's learning a musical instrument, a new language, or a professional skill, habits play a vital role in improvement.

## How to start a new habit

Now that you know why they’re good for you, let’s focus on how you can develop your own good habits. Whether it’s getting started with exercise or reducing your screen time, these tips can help you create a new routine of your own.

* **Make a decision.** Think about what you want to achieve and decide what habit can help you get there. For example, if you want to improve your health, you might choose to make exercise a new habit.
* **Be specific and realistic.** For your habit to “stick” it’s important to be specific. Rather than say “I’m going to exercise more,” determine how often and how much you will exercise. You may start by setting a goal of exercising five times each week for 30 minutes.
* **Start small.** It’s important to start small and gradually increase your efforts. If you have just begun to exercise, don’t expect to run a marathon in a month. To stay motivated, be sure to make it something you can achieve.
* **Make it part of your schedule.** To commit to it, schedule time for your new habit. If you decide to exercise four times mark that time on your calendar. Having it as part of your schedule makes it part of your daily to-do list.
* **Stick to it.** Set a goal for yourself and stick to your plan. Don’t let distractions or emotions keep you from sticking to your new routine. The more you repeat a behavior, the easier it will get. Don’t give up!
* **Let others know your intentions.** When you tell others about your decision, it creates a network of support. When people encourage and support you, it can make all the difference when it comes to a new goal or routine.

## How long does it take to form a habit

You may have heard it only takes as little as three days to form a new habit, but that may not be quite enough time. The fact is every habit and each person is different. The time it takes to develop that habit will vary.

A [well-known study](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/ejsp.674 "European Journal of Social Psychology: How Habits are Formed") reports that it takes between 18 and 254 days to build a new habit. It also concluded that it takes 66 days on average for a habit to become automatic.

The take-away? It takes time and effort for a habit to become natural to you. To make it a little easier, the American Heart Association offers the Healthy for Good program, with many tips and tricks to ensure your success in developing your healthy habits. You can learn more and sign up at the [American Heart Association's website](https://www.heart.org/en/healthy-living/healthy-lifestyle/habits "American Heart Association: Making Habits Stick").

## How to break a bad habit

It can be hard to stop doing something that has become part of your nature. But once you recognize a bad habit, there are ways you can overcome it.

* **Acknowledge the bad habit.** The first step to change is recognizing the issue. If you know your habit is affecting you in a negative way, acknowledge it and decide to make a change for the better.
* **Identify your triggers.** Typically, bad habits are triggered by something. For instance, if you smoke, your normal routine may be to light up after a meal. Knowing that food is your trigger can help you change your behavior.
* **Create a new routine to replace the old.** It’s helpful to change a bad habit by replacing it with a positive one. If you have a habit of stepping outside for a cigarette after a meal, switch it up. Instead of smoking, take a walk, phone a friend, or clean the kitchen. Swapping one routine for another is helpful.
* **Be kind to yourself.** It’s hard to break a habit, and it is easy to fall back into old patterns. When that happens, remind yourself that you are trying to change and focus on getting back to your new routine. [Mindfulness](https://www.brownhealth.org/be-well/practice-mindfulness-dont-just-do-something-stand-there "Practice Mindfulness: Don’t Just Do Something, Stand There!") is a great way to keep yourself focused and motivated.

Our [Be Well](/be-well "Welcome to Be Well") health and wellness blog has many other tips to help you live your best life. Be sure to sign up for our email newsletter for more great information too.

## 'Single': Aima Baig's Instagram story triggers social media speculation

![](http://www.magtheweekly.com/assets/uploads/updates/2026-10-21/27758_4332380_updates.jpg)

Singer Aima Baig has left social media in confusion after dropping a cryptic response to a post about her "relationship status", fuelling speculation that her marriage to fashion designer Zain Ahmad has come to an end. Rumours of the couple’s separation continue to swirl online, with the singer’s reaction sparking fresh speculation. Aima reshared an Instagram story, which stated: “Aima Baig casually making a statement with a caption that declares her relationship status to be ‘single’”.

In response, the vocalist conceded the claim, but she neither directly mentioned her divorce nor shared more details. She only wrote: “The truth 100%.” However, the response prompted "curiosity" among social media users. The couple tied the knot in August 2025.

## When Pakistan Loses, Its Cricket Fans Disappear: Wasim Akram

![](http://www.magtheweekly.com/assets/uploads/updates/2026-10-21/27754_594447_updates.jpg)

Cricket legend Wasim Akram believes Pakistan’s declining on-field performance is affecting the younger generation’s interest in the sport. “When the team doesn’t perform well, the followers disappear,” he said in a recent interview. Akram, who never pushed his sons to follow in his cricketing footsteps, noted that children of celebrities often face immense pressure when pursuing their parents’ professions. “I never pushed them towards playing cricket. They could do whatever they wanted to do,” he said.

Reflecting on his playing days in the 1980s and 1990s, Akram recalled a time when cricket stars were national heroes and fans gathered to welcome the team and seek autographs. “We were their heroes, Captain Imran Khan and his entire team,” he remembered.

Despite the contrast with today, Akram said he is content with life beyond his playing career. “You can’t change the past, you can only plan the future and you have to live in the present.”

# Everything New on Prime Video This Week — And the 3 Titles Worth Adding to Your Watchlist

![Parade](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/logos/light/aol_parade_744.png)
![](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/10/30/90d04e0b-3de4-3832-9d2f-97fe1689ed38/261e9312-16a7-41ec-9253-260a7edce5ae.jpg)

Prime Video’s lineup this weekend bridges late-fall suspense with the ultimate procedural comfort marathon. You can get into the Halloween spirit with some of the streamer’s original horror and thriller series. And November kicks off with an iconic FOX series arriving in its entirety.Here are the top three TV shows available on Prime Video this weekend (Oct. 30 – Nov. 1, 2026).

**🎬**[**SIGN UP for Parade’s Daily newsletter to get the latest pop culture news & celebrity interviews delivered right to your inbox**](https://parade.com/newsletters/daily?utm_source=article&utm_medium=top) **🎬**

## New on Prime Video This Weekend (Oct. 30 – Nov. 1, 2026)

### *Carrie*

Available to stream throughout the weekend following its mid-October premiere, this eight-episode limited series offers a modern adaptation of **Stephen King’**s landmark 1974 epistolary novel. Developed by horror auteur **Mike Flanagan**, the drama chronicles the life of Carrie White, an isolated and relentlessly bullied high school student raised by an overbearing, severely devout mother.

When Carrie begins to manifest destructive telekinetic abilities, the escalating psychological torment from her peers pushes her toward a fateful confrontation at the senior prom. Flanagan’s adaptation expands King’s source text into a character-driven examination of trauma, adolescent cruelty, and repressed power. For people seeking psychological horror after Halloween night, the full miniseries is available to stream in its entirety.

**Related:** **[The Best Stephen King Adaptations to Stream This Fall](https://parade.com/tv/best-will-they-wont-they-tv-couples)**

### *Bones* (Seasons 1–12)

![](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/10/30/90d04e0b-3de4-3832-9d2f-97fe1689ed38/6e9b7fe8-bb35-4225-a0eb-41e3407bedbf.jpg)

Arriving Sunday, Nov. 1, the complete run of FOX’s long-running procedural drama *Bones* joins Prime Video’s streaming catalog. Spanning 12 seasons and 246 episodes, the series follows forensic anthropologist Dr. Temperance “Bones” Brennan (**Emily Deschanel)** and former Army sniper turned FBI Special Agent Seeley Booth (**David Boreanaz**). Together, they solve complex murder cases by examining the decomposed and skeletal remains of victims that conventional forensic methods cannot identify.

Backed by an ensemble cast featuring **Michaela Conlin**, **T.J. Thyne**, **Tamara Taylor** and **John Francis Daley**, the series remains celebrated for the slow-burning chemistry between its two mismatched leads. Having every season available in one place makes it a reliable, long-term binge for crime-drama enthusiasts as November begins.

**Related:** **[Ranking the Best Will-They-Won’t-They Couples on TV](https://parade.com/tv/best-will-they-wont-they-tv-couples)**

### *Neagley*

![](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/10/30/90d04e0b-3de4-3832-9d2f-97fe1689ed38/f657c585-a28e-45a4-9bf7-da6735b8b8fe.jpg)

Expanding the world of *Reacher*, the eight-episode spinoff *Neagley* centers on fan-favorite private investigator Frances Neagley (**Maria Sten**). When an old friend from her past dies under highly suspicious circumstances, Neagley leaves her routine corporate assignments behind to launch a relentless, unsanctioned personal investigation.

Created for television by **Nick Santora** and **Nicholas Wootton**, the spinoff brings the character’s formidable military police tradecraft and guarded emotional interior into the spotlight without relying on Jack Reacher’s physical presence to drive the plot. For viewers looking for an adrenaline-fueled procedural mystery featuring tactical combat, sharp investigative instincts, and a gritty narrative, all episodes of *Neagley* are currently available to stream.

**[Related: This Fan-Favorite Book Adaptation Isn’t Slowing Down; Prime Video Locks In Season 6 Already](https://parade.com/tv/reacher-renewed-season-6-prime-video)**

resource.content:
![Quantcast](//pixel.quantserve.com/pixel/p-CWej69n6WDWnD.gif)
![Bloody Disgusting Logo](https://i0.wp.com/bloody-disgusting.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/BD_LOGO-e1658360764590.webp?fit=2000%2C467&ssl=1)

# Ted Raimi Reveals His Essential Halloween Horror Watchlist

![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/bb1cb3d18242b86f803dfa56ac18286e5829b79c2e03924c921c04c6222de3db?s=44&d=mm&r=r)
![](https://i0.wp.com/bloody-disgusting.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/The-Fly.jpg?resize=1330%2C748&ssl=1)

The Fly (1986)

**Ted Raimi** is a living horror legend, an icon of the genre with plenty of credits to his name both in front of and behind the camera, and this Halloween, he’s invading your living room. 

Today, **October 30**, Screambox will premiere [***Your Dearest Darkest Friend***](https://bloody-disgusting.com/exclusives/3971951/ted-raimi-invites-horror-icons-into-his-haunted-manor-in-your-dearest-darkest-friend-trailer/), a new talk show hosted and created by Raimi, which follows the actor, producer, director, and writer as he simultaneously plays classic horror host and in-depth interviewer. Each episode features a conversation with a fellow horror icon, covering everything from the trajectory of their careers to the craft they apply to each project, supported by custom-created cocktails and, naturally, a puppet co-host named Mort (voiced by [**Ed Larson**](https://bloody-disgusting.com/exclusives/3969703/ted-raimis-your-dearest-darkest-friend-last-podcast-on-left/)). 

The show’s premiere means that Raimi fans will spend a portion of their Halloween weekend with him and his guests, but how does Ted Raimi like to spend Halloween? What are his must-watch films that he resurrects every single October? 

Speaking to Bloody Disgusting via Zoom, Raimi explained that his Halloween is not complete without a few “tragedies,” movies where good doesn’t always prevail over evil, and the heroes actually often end up in a darker place than when they began. 

“The ones I watch every year are ones where the hero in the story fails miserably at the end,” Raimi said. “I do love gore, and I’ll always watch gore, but the ones I always go back to are character-centric horror, where the hero attempts something so outlandish and fails in a horror way. Those are the ones I love the most.”

![Your Dearest Darkest Friend Trailer](https://i0.wp.com/bloody-disgusting.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/YDDF-Episode-1.png?resize=1024%2C573&ssl=1)

![Your Dearest Darkest Friend Trailer](https://i0.wp.com/bloody-disgusting.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/YDDF-Episode-1.png?resize=1024%2C573&ssl=1)

So, which movies are included in his list of must-watch character pieces? 

“I would say number one is Cronenberg’s [***The Fly***](https://bloody-disgusting.com/editorials/3712686/david-cronenbergs-the-fly-remake-effects/), the remake. Also [***The Dead Zone***](https://bloody-disgusting.com/editorials/3768577/the-king-of-1983-cujo-the-dead-zone-and-christine-at-40/), another one where the character attempts everything he can and fails horribly at the end. [***Angel Heart***](https://bloody-disgusting.com/home-video/3715540/horror-noir-angel-heart-heading-to-4k-ultra-hd-for-first-time-ever-with-limited-edition-steelbook/), a detective-story failure. [***The Serpent and the Rainbow***](https://bloody-disgusting.com/editorials/3481377/celebrating-30-years-wes-cravens-serpent-rainbow/) is another must-watch for the very same reason. I always go back to that during Halloween. [***Jacob’s Ladder***](https://bloody-disgusting.com/movie/3911559/jacobs-ladder-how-an-lsd-trip-and-a-dream-of-hell-led-to-the-mind-bending-cult-classic/), total soldier failure, but great. I love tragedies in horror, horror and tragedy.

“Another one I like is an early **John Frankenheimer** movie called [***Seconds***](https://bloody-disgusting.com/news/3363684/seconds-get-masters-cinema-uk-release/). It’s from 1966; you gotta be in the right place to dig that. [***The Vanishing***](https://bloody-disgusting.com/editorials/3809391/religious-horror-immaculate-companion-watch-guide/), I just watched that one the other day. The *Spoorloos* one from 1988. That is a character whose curiosity truly kills him in the end, in a gruesome way. Sorry, spoiler alert, but I’m not going to say how he dies. Finally, another Cronenberg film, [***The Shrouds***](https://bloody-disgusting.com/reviews/3830222/the-shrouds-review-david-cronenberg-plays-his-greatest-hits-tiff/), which came out a couple years ago, same thing. My girlfriend and I love that movie, and I’ll watch that a million times or more. Those movies are probably my top, whatever that is, 8 to 10 pictures.”

So, why does Raimi tend to go for tragedy rather than, say, a horror-comedy or something lighter? Because on Halloween, Ted Raimi likes to be truly, deeply scared. 

“Those are the things that frighten me the most,” Raimi explained. “I like a mixture of human tragedy with gore and body horror. You can always divorce yourself from gore when you get out of a movie. It’s like a roller-coaster ride. I love it, but you can divorce yourself from it. The movies that stay with you are the ones that also have personal tragedy in them.

“A good example is [***The Hitcher***](https://bloody-disgusting.com/editorials/3652798/hitcher-turns-35-remembering-rutger-hauers-terrifying-performance-feb-21/) with **Rutger Hauer** and **C. Thomas Howell**. It’s another good example of that, where C. Thomas Howell is just a kid, and he’s just trying to drive a car across the country. That’s it. That’s all he wants. Everything horrible happens to him, and he loses at the end. Those movies really stick with me because of that.”

According to the man himself, if you go to Ted Raimi’s house on Halloween, you’re going to get a lot of movies that end on very sad notes. Fortunately, as with [*Your Dearest, Darkest Friend*](https://bloody-disgusting.com/interviews/3973736/ted-raimi-on-new-screambox-talk-show-your-dearest-darkest-friend/), you’ll also get cocktails to wash those movies down. So, what’s Raimi drinking during all of these cinematic tragedies?

“Everything,” Raimi said with a laugh. “For these movies, it’s usually classics. I don’t like too many fancy drinks with my horror movies. I’ll either do Old Fashioneds or Gin Martinis with olives, never with a twist because I like the tartness of the olives. You need that. If I drink something that’s too elaborate during a horror movie, I just focus on the drink, and I don’t want to do that.”

### **Ted Raimi’s Halloween Watchlist:**

**1. The Fly**  
**2. The Dead Zone**  
**3. Angel Heart**  
**4. The Serpent and the Rainbow**  
**5. Jacob’s Ladder**  
**6. Seconds**  
**7. The Vanishing**  
**8. The Shrouds**  
**9. The Hitcher**

***Your Dearest, Darkest Friend with Ted Raimi* premieres October 30 on Screambox. New episodes will release every Friday.**

resource.title: The Most Fashionable Erotic Thrillers to Add to Your Halloween Watchlist
resource.content:
# Fashionable, Freaky Erotic Thrillers for Your Halloween Watchlist

by [Natalie Michie](/profile/natalie-michie-476049455)

---

Madonna in 'Body of Evidence.' Murray Close/Sygma/Getty Images

If you’re looking to be seduced, scared, and sartorially inspired, then the erotic thriller is what you seek. A kinky successor to the neo-noir, the subgenre boomed in the 1990s and came to define an entire era of sexy cinema. Filled with double entendres and fatalistic love-making, the erotic thriller is hot, campy, and brimming with excellent outfits.

Often following an ethically ambiguous leading lady and a man who is wont to be fooled, these films use fashion as a plot device. Madonna’s on-trial character wears prim pearls to convey her innocence in *Body of Evidence*. In *Sliver*, Sharon Stone unbuttons her LBD in a dangerously public setting. And we all understand the cultural significance of the white dress in *Basic Instinct.*

Below, the most fashionable erotic thrillers to get you into the come-hither Halloween spirit.

## *Basic Instinct* (1992)

Shutterstock

The white *Basic Instinct* dress is so iconic that Sharon Stone [keeps it locked in a safe](https://deadline.com/2025/03/sharon-stone-what-happened-basic-instinct-interrogation-dress-1236306842/). Famously, in the film, it’s worn by her character Catherine, a moneyed crime novelist who appears highly suspicious after her boyfriend is murdered in the same way as a character from her book. She looks guilty, but she doesn’t mind. Catherine glides around in beige loungewear and airy slip dresses, lighting cigarettes in no-smoking areas and passing lie detector tests with imperceptible ease. But it’s her subtly sheer ivory slip, worn during a police interrogation scene, that best sums up her enigmatic allure. It remains a symbol of provocation—so much so that Demna opened his [debut fall 2026 Gucci show](https://www.wmagazine.com/fashion/gucci-fall-2026-demna-debut-runway-photos) with an homage.

Snap/Shutterstock

StudioCanal/Shutterstock

1/2

## *Single White Female* (1992)

Columbia/Kobal/Shutterstock

The first detail that jumps out about *Single White Female* protagonist Allie (Bridget Fonda) is her red bowl cut. A choice! That specific look, along with her enviable wardrobe of power dressing pieces, becomes central to the film’s spine-chilling plot. After leaving her cheating fiancé and moving into a Manhattan apartment alone, she puts an ad in the paper for a roommate. Along comes Hedy (Jennifer Jason Leigh), an awkward but innocuous-seeming bookstore clerk. As they spend more time together, Hedy starts to copy Allie’s hair, wear Allie’s clothes, and ultimately steal Allie’s identity. They do, in fact, both end up with red bowl cuts, which some might say is two too many.

**Where to watch: Tubi**

Columbia/Kobal/Shutterstock

Columbia/Kobal/Shutterstock

1/2

## *Sliver* (1993)

Paramount/Kobal/Shutterstock

Released just one year after *Basic Instinct*, *Sliver* finds Sharon Stone swapping her blonde blowout for a precise bob. She plays Carly Norris, a career-minded book editor who moves into a sleek Manhattan high-rise, only to find the building is plagued with mysterious murders. Shot through windows, mirrors, and grainy video footage, *Sliver* embraces the extremes of people watching other people, and Carly’s outfits play into that theme. In one high-stakes scene, she unbuttons her dress in the middle of a fine-dining restaurant on a dare from her possibly murderous date (William Baldwin).

**Where to watch: Paramount+**

Suzanne Tenner/Paramount/Kobal/Shutterstock

## *Body of Evidence* (1993)

Murray Close/Sygma/Getty Images

*Body of Evidence* finds a pre-*Erotica* Madonna playing Rebecca Carlson, a woman on trial. Her supposed crime? Murdering her lover, an elderly millionaire, by giving him a heart attack in bed. Rebecca insists she’s innocent, but as her relationship with her married lawyer (Willem Dafoe) intensifies, it’s obvious her morals are muddied. In the courtroom, her rotation of tailored blazers and prim pearls—sometimes with a beret thrown in for good measure—feels like a put-on performance. Especially since she doesn’t seem to care much about her clothes; they’re always being ripped off.

**Where to watch: Tubi**

Dino De Laurentiis/Kobal/Shutterstock

Dino De Laurentiis/Kobal/Shutterstock

1/2

## *Bound* (1996)

Dino De Laurentiis/Summit/Kobal/Shutterstock

In this tension-filled lesbian thriller, there are two aesthetics at play. Violet (Jennifer Tilly) is the breathy, lingerie-clad femme fatale. Donning lace LBDs, gauzy nylons, and *Betty Boop* curls, she’s stuck in a loveless relationship with an abusive mob boss. When she meets Corky (Gina Ghershion)—an ex-con hired to do work on the apartment next door—things take a heated turn. Fresh out of prison, Corky is hot and vaguely unwashed, sporting a terrible barbed-wire tattoo, a stringy pixie, and spiky earrings she uses to pick locks. They hatch a plan to steal millions, things get bloody fast, and they both look very hot in the process.

**Where to watch: Pluto TV**

Dino De Laurentiis/Summit/Kobal/Shutterstock

Dino De Laurentiis/Summit Ent/Kobal/Shutterstock

## *Eyes Wide Shut* (1999)

Shutterstock

In the opening scene of Stanley Kubrick’s *Eyes Wide Shut*, a camera follows Nicole Kidman from behind as she [drops her John Galliano](https://www.instagram.com/p/DR-ZmLTkpI-/?img_index=1) dress to the floor and stands naked in her room. The shot sets up the film’s voyeuristic sensuality, and the LBD—Kidman’s own—has become a piece of fashion history. “The scene where I drop the dress...that was me. That wasn’t written. That was my dress from my closet,” she said to the *[Los Angeles Times](http://nt-arts/movies/story/2024-07-16/the-1999-project-eyes-wide-shut-nicole-kidman-tom-cruise-standley-kubrick-sydney-pollack)* [in 2024,](http://nt-arts/movies/story/2024-07-16/the-1999-project-eyes-wide-shut-nicole-kidman-tom-cruise-standley-kubrick-sydney-pollack) adding that she told Kubrick at the time, “This is how I take off the dress, Stanley.” While filming, she worked with costume designer Merit Allen and her personal costume consultant, L’Wren Scott, to pull pieces from her own closet. Perhaps the most memorable outfit, though, is her [still-coveted](https://wwd.com/fashion-news/fashion-scoops/feature/hanro-tank-top-nicole-kidman-1234949783/) white Hanro tank top and briefs.

**Where to watch: HBO Max**

Warner Bros/Kobal/Shutterstock

* It was the first wave of arrests under Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s govt, with about 400 protesters present
* ‘It’s a terrible shame that people who are trying to stop a genocide are being arrested,” says demonstrator Sue Morhall, 79

Updated 31 October 2026 13:40

[Arab News](/authors/arab-news)

[Follow](https://twitter.com/intent/follow?screen_name=arabnews)

LONDON: Dozens of people were arrested on Saturday at the US Embassy in London at a mass demonstration opposing the proscription of Palestine Action, The Guardian reported.

The wave of arrests was the first under Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government, with organizers estimating that about 400 people took part in the rally.

Demonstrators gathered outside the building in Nine Elms and held signs that read: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”

Another protest took place outside the US Consulate in Edinburgh, where protesters held a vigil in support of the banned group.

London’s Metropolitan Police warned people against taking part ahead of the demonstration.

Protesters would “face arrest as part of a robust policing operation” and those “playing a key role in organising the event, giving instructions to others and/or providing logistical support” would likely be committing an offense, the force said.

Adam Slonecki, the police commander in charge of the operation, said: “All those intending on coming to this event know that supporting a proscribed organisation is unlawful — they are essentially meeting to purposefully commit a crime.”

The Met was “terrified of facilitating US embarrassment,” said Defend Our Juries, organizers of the protest.

A spokesperson for the group said: “The Met police’s overzealous response outside the US Embassy today only serves to further expose how far authorities in the UK will go to appease American interests. Israel’s war crimes that have caused death and injury to thousands could not happen without the US’ approval.”

The arrests came ahead of a Nov. 4 appeal at the supreme court against Palestine Action’s designation as a terror group.

More than 160 people were arrested or reported for summons last month at a similar demonstration in support of the banned group outside the Labour Party’s annual conference in Liverpool.

Palestine Action was proscribed in June 2025. Expressing support for the group is an offense under the Terrorism Act.

At Saturday’s protest, a retired lawyer, Charles Allison, 75, traveled from Cumbria to attend because he “feared for our liberties,” the Press Association reported.

“I decided that I ought to try and do something, and this is the little bit that I’m doing. I fear for our civil liberties, which are being devalued and watered down, even by this new Labour government,” he added.

“So, I’m dejected, but enthused that there are so many wonderful people protesting.”

Meanwhile, Sue Morhall, 79, another protester outside the US Embassy, told The Guardian: “The US is complicit in most of the wars that are going on. I just feel the leaders of this world, including Trump, need to know that people are so against what’s happening in Gaza.”

Morhall said she believes Burnham may rescind Palestine Action’s proscription, and that she had been arrested “five or six” times at previous demonstrations against the ban.

“It’s a terrible shame that people who are trying to stop a genocide are being arrested … it’s the principle, and this is one that I feel very strongly about,” she added.

Bill White, a 72-year-old church reverend that held an “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action” sign, said: “I’m appalled that Britain is helping facilitate the genocide that is happening in Palestine. We supply weapons that are being used on Palestinians.”

As a person of faith, White said he had “no choice” but to take part in the protest, adding: “This is the right thing to do. There’s a bad law and it is wrong to criminalise people that are trying to prevent genocide.

“How can I not be here?”
