# 50 best films to watch on Netflix right now

Some of the best movies on Netflix right now include Wicked: Part I, Brooklyn, Anora, Teenage Wasteland and Wonder Woman. Updated weekly.

* [Radio Times staff](/author/rtstaff/)

Published: Friday, 16 October 2026 at 6:13 pm

50 items

[Subscribe to Radio Times: 10 weeks for £10, including the Christmas double issue](https://www.radiotimes.com/subscribe/?utm_medium=brandsite&utm_source=brandsite&utm_content=promotional-link&utm_campaign=sit-christmas-oct-2026)

* [Share on facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https://www.radiotimes.com/movies/what-to-watch/best-movies-netflix-watch-now/)
* [Share on twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=50%20best%20films%20to%20watch%20on%20Netflix%20right%20now%0A%0A&url=https://www.radiotimes.com/movies/what-to-watch/best-movies-netflix-watch-now/)
* [Share on pinterest](https://www.pinterest.com/pin/create/button/?url=https://www.radiotimes.com/movies/what-to-watch/best-movies-netflix-watch-now/&media=&description=50%20best%20films%20to%20watch%20on%20Netflix%20right%20now)
* [Share on reddit](https://www.reddit.com/submit?url=https://www.radiotimes.com/movies/what-to-watch/best-movies-netflix-watch-now/&title=50%20best%20films%20to%20watch%20on%20Netflix%20right%20now)
* [Email to a friend](mailto:?subject=On RadioTimes today:&body=I saw this and thought it might interest you...%0A%0Ahttps://www.radiotimes.com/movies/what-to-watch/best-movies-netflix-watch-now/)

If you're a film fan and find yourself wading through [Netflix](https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/netflix/)'s extensive library without knowing what to choose, let Radio Times's experts help you uncover the platform's best picks.

Godzilla Minus One is a standalone film that takes us back to basics in post-war Japan. But the latest entry in this 70 year old franchise is anything but basic. It follows a former WWII kamikaze pilot named Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who ended up on Odo Island just as a monster soon to be named Godzilla shows up and destroys the place. Only Kōichi and mechanic Sōsaku Tachibana (Munetaka Aoki) survived, but even two years later, the guilt of surviving when the others didn't still plagues his every moment.

A recent arrival for all the family is Wicked: Part One, the spectacular musical fantasy revealing the untold story of Oz’s witches, as the misunderstood Elphaba (Cynthia Erivo) and popular Glinda (Ariana Grande) forge an unlikely friendship that changes both their lives.

New to the platform is gripping political thriller Animals, directed by and starring Ben Affleck. When the teenage son of a Los Angeles mayoral candidate is kidnapped, he and his wife are plunged into a desperate race to secure the ransom, uncovering a web of secrets, lies and moral compromises that threaten both their family and political future. Co-starring Kerry Washington, Gillian Anderson and Steven Yeun, the tense drama combines family stakes with high-pressure political intrigue.

In romantic drama Brooklyn, Saoirse Ronan plays a young woman torn between two lovers – one in an America easing its way out of the 1950s straitjacket, the other back in good old, safe old Ireland. Whichever way she jumps, there will probably be tears before bedtime, possibly preceded by a nice cup of cocoa.

The Suicide Squad spin-off [Birds of Prey: and the Fantabulous Emancipation of One Harley Quinn](https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/sci-fi/birds-of-prey-soundtrack/) sees the eponymous hero (played by Margot Robbie) team up with vigilantes Black Canary (Jurnee Smollett-Bell), Huntress (Mary Elizabeth Winstead) and Renee Montoya (Rosie Perez) to protect a young girl from Ewan McGregor's sleek villain Black Mask. To make matters worse, Batman is missing from Gotham City so crime is running rampant...

The 1994 Formula One season was overshadowed by horror at the San Marino Grand Prix, but it also saw one of the sport’s greats driving into the spotlight. Cracking new Netflix film Schumacher ’94: the Birth of a Legend digs into the archive to tell the story of Michael Schumacher’s rapid rise.

Read on for our latest picks of the best films on Netflix – from recent releases like [Train Dreams](https://www.radiotimes.com/movies/how-to-watch-train-dreams/) and [Remarkably Bright Creatures](https://www.radiotimes.com/movies/remarkably-bright-creatures-netflix-cast/) to classics like We Don't Live Here Anymore and originals such as [Roma](https://www.radiotimes.com/movies/roma-netflix-movie-review-a-striking-heartfelt-historical-drama/) – or head over to our guides to the [best series on Netflix](/tv/what-to-watch-tv/best-tv-series-netflix-shows-updated/) and [best documentaries on Netflix](https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/best-netflix-documentaries-to-watch-right-now/).

Alternatively, check out our helpful list of [Netflix secret codes](https://www.radiotimes.com/technology/netflix-secret-codes-uk/), which can help you unlock hidden movies and TV shows.

*Updated weekly.*

Showing 1 to 24 of 50 results

* [Godzilla Minus One](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-usvsp8/godzilla-minus-one/)

  2023

  Adventure

  Fantasy

  12A

  Monster horror starring Ryunosuke Kamiki. Towards the end of the Second World War, kamikaze pilot Koichi witnesses a devastating attack on a small island by a gigantic, lizard-like sea creature dubbed "*gojira*". Years later, the same creature re-emerges and begins to wreak terrible destruction on Japan. Koichi is haunted by his failure to act the first time around - can he now step up and help to defeat the monster?
* [Wicked: Part I](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-fhrjst/wicked/)

  2024

  Fantasy

  Music

  PG

  Fantasy musical starring Cynthia Erivo and Ariana Grande-Butera. Elphaba Thropp is an outcast among the citizens of Oz due to her green skin and magical powers. When she arrives at the prestigious Shiz University, she is given a chance to develop her abilities and finds an unlikely friend in the popular Galinda. But something's rotten in the state of Oz, and the two young women arrive at a crossroads from which there'll be no turning back.
* [Brooklyn](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-129x1g/brooklyn/)

  2015

  Drama

  Romance

  12A

  Romantic drama starring Saoirse Ronan and Domhnall Gleeson. County Wexford, 1950: young Eilis Lacey is sponsored for a job in America by a visiting priest and so she leaves her mother and sister for New York. The metropolis offers the chance of a career and romance, but the big city can be a lonely place for a small-town girl.
* [Animals](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-xvztdw/animals/)

  2026

  Thriller

  Crime/detective

  15

  Ben Affleck returns to the director's chair for the first time since 2023's sporting drama Air to helm, co-write and star in this tense political thriller. Los Angeles mayoral candidate Mark Kimball (Ben Affleck) has invested the majority of his family's personal fortune into his high-profile campaign, supported by his wife Abigail (Kerry Washington) and son Denny (Christopher Woodley). When Denny is kidnapped and held for ransom, the Kimballs have a few precious hours to conjure up money they don't have. Mysterious fixer Dayle (Gillian Anderson) is drafted in to oversee the negotiation, which may involve Mark and Abigail revealing the dark secrets they never intended to bring to light
* [The Lego Movie](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-br1i8z/the-lego-movie/)

  2014

  Animation

  Comedy

  U

  Animated comedy adventure featuring the voices of Will Ferrell and Chris Pratt. When the evil Lord Business attempts to take over the Lego world using a mystical super-weapon called the Kragle, it falls to an unlikely hero, construction worker Emmet, to save the day.
* [Wonder Woman](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-fdtfc6/wonder-woman/)

  2017

  Adventure

  Fantasy

  12

  Fantasy action adventure starring Gal Gadot and Chris Pine. Young Diana has been raised a warrior on the secret island of Themyscira, shielded from the perils of the real world. When she rescues an American pilot whose plane crashes off the coast, Diana learns about the horrors of the First World War, and leaves the island with him to fight for peace and justice.
* [Ted](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-mffcgw/ted/)

  2012

  Comedy

  Fantasy

  18

  Comedy starring Mark Wahlberg, Mila Kunis and the voice of Seth MacFarlane. When young John Bennett's wish that his beloved toy bear Ted could come to life is granted, the two become inseparable. But as they grow older, although not necessarily more mature, the potty-mouthed furry one starts to get in the way of John's other relationships.
* [Birds of Prey: and the Fantabulous Emancipation of One Harley Quinn](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-d91xd8/birds-of-prey-and-the-fantabulous-emancipation-of-one-harley-quinn/)

  2020

  Adventure

  Fantasy

  15

  Having split from The Joker, psychotic psychiatrist Harley Quinn joins forces with other superheroes to save a girl from the clutches of the villainous Roman Sionis, aka Black Mask. Director Cathy Yan's fantasy adventure spun off from Suicide Squad, starring Margot Robbie, Mary Elizabeth Winstead and Ewan McGregor
* [Crazy Rich Asians](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-jprnqf/crazy-rich-asians/)

  2018

  Comedy

  Drama

  12

  Romantic comedy starring Constance Wu, Henry Golding and Michelle Yeoh. New Yorker Rachel Chu travels to Singapore with her partner, Nick, for a friend's wedding, and discovers that Nick's family is hugely wealthy. They also expect him to remain in Singapore to inherit their hotel business - a plan that, as Nick's imperious mother Eleanor makes quite clear, does not involve Rachel.
* [We Don't Live Here Anymore](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-lthus8/we-dont-live-here-anymore/)

  2003

  Drama

  Romance

  15

  An academic who neglects his alcoholic wife, and routinely sleeps with his students, begins an affair with a bored housewife - but the pair are unaware their own partners are also about to start a relationship with each other, and that their children know all about their parents' lies and infidelities. Drama, starring Mark Ruffalo, Naomi Watts, Laura Dern and Peter Krause
* [Schumacher '94: the Birth of a Legend](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-h7mjsr/schumacher-94-the-birth-of-a-legend/)

  2026

  Documentary

  Sport

  12

  Michael Schumacher's first World Championship win roars to life through personal interviews and archival footage of the legendary 1994 Formula 1 season
* [The Unforgivable](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-9zoom4/the-unforgivable/)

  2021

  Crime/detective

  Drama

  15

  Convict Ruth Slater is released back into society after serving a long sentence for a violent crime. She reluctantly returns home to track down her younger sister Katie, who she was forced to leave behind. Back in the place where her life whirled out of control, Ruth encounters anger, disbelief and harsh judgement.
* [The Deepest Breath](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-kc4wro/the-deepest-breath/)

  2023

  Documentary

  Travel

  12A

  Bonded by their love of freediving, a record-setting champion and a heroic safety diver try to make history with a remarkable feat, ready to risk it all.
* [Piece by Piece](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-kc4i28/piece-by-piece/)

  2024

  Animation

  Family

  PG

  Pharrell Williams tells the story of his life - through the lens of Lego animation. With an all-star cast, including Kendrick Lamar, Gwen Stefani and Snoop Dogg
* [Dune: Part Two](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-pqqeht/dune-part-two/)

  2023

  Sci-fi

  Adventure

  12

  Epic sci-fi drama starring Timothée Chalamet and Zendaya. With the evil Harkonnen family back in charge of Arrakis, deposed heir Paul Atreides and his mother have taken refuge with the native Fremen in the planet's perilous desert wasteland. Paul becomes close with Fremen warrior Chani and begins to demonstrate powers that persuade her people to aid in the young man's plan to avenge his father and take back control.
* [Small Things like These](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-lblgct/small-things-like-these/)

  2024

  Drama

  12A

  Historical drama starring Cillian Murphy. It's Christmas 1985 in County Wexford, where coal merchant Bill, devoted father to five daughters but still troubled by a traumatic past, chances upon an imprisoned girl in freezing conditions when delivering to the local convent laundry. It's soon apparent this is just one part of a larger system of church oppression that threatens to blow his family life apart.
* [Remarkably Bright Creatures](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-l455fj/remarkably-bright-creatures/)

  2026

  Comedy

  Drama

  12

  While working nights at a small-town aquarium, a widow bonds with a clever octopus and an adrift young man in this moving drama based on the bestseller.
* [Frankenstein](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-kyqq9u/frankenstein/)

  2025

  Horror

  Fantasy

  15

  Fantasy horror starring Oscar Isaac and Jacob Elordi. In 1857, a Danish polar exploration ship rescues Baron Victor Frankenstein from the ice and the crew is attacked by a powerful man-like monster. Frankenstein recounts the story of how he created the frightful Creature by harnessing the power of the elements. However, his version of events differs from that of the Creature, which has its own account of life under the maniacal scientist.
* [Teenage Wasteland](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-ksf2j2/teenage-wasteland/)

  2025

  Documentary

  In 1991, an eccentric teacher and his students exposed a toxic waste conspiracy through a DIY documentary. Decades later, they look back on its impact.
* [Anora](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-9plxbc/anora/)

  2024

  Drama

  Comedy

  18

  Comedy drama starring Mikey Madison. New York erotic dancer Ani is overjoyed when a young and extremely wealthy Russian client, Ivan, proposes to her. The two are quickly married, but this fairy-tale ending curdles when it transpires that the immature Ivan has a powerful family that wants the union annulled - immediately.
* [Dìdi](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-3f16wt/ddi/)

  2024

  Comedy

  Drama

  15

  During the last month of summer before high school begins, a Taiwanese American boy decides to learn what his family can't teach him: how to skate, how to flirt, and how to love your mom. Comedy, starring Izaac Wang, Joan Chen, Shirley Chen and Zhang Li Hua
* [Uncut Gems](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-xh05il/uncut-gems/)

  2019

  Thriller

  Crime/detective

  15

  Wheeler-dealer jeweller Howard Ratner has torn apart his family by moving in with mistress and lover Julia. He is heavily debted to loan shark Arno. The jeweller hopes to turn around his fortunes by submitting a black opal for auction, which he believes should be valued at one million dollars. Crime drama, starring Adam Sandler, Julia Fox, Idina Menzel, Mesfin Lamengo and Sun Zhi Hua-Hilton
* [Private Life](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-cjaw73/private-life/)

  2018

  Comedy

  Drama

  15

  Struggling to conceive, a couple in their 40s are almost out of options -- until a sliver of hope arrives in the form of their visiting step-niece.
* [The Wild Robot](https://www.radiotimes.com/movie-guide/b-jhlgxg/the-wild-robot/)

  2024

  Adventure

  Animation

  U

  Animated adventure featuring the voices of Lupita Nyong'o, Kit Connor and Pedro Pascal. Washed up on the shore of an island, robot "Roz" learns to cope with the environment. When she encounters orphaned gosling Brightbill, Roz and wily fox Fink join forces to raise the runt.

By
[Naman Ramachandran](https://variety.com/author/saharanaman-ramachandran/)

### [Naman Ramachandran](https://variety.com/author/saharanaman-ramachandran/)

Indonesian filmmaker Ariani Darmawan stepped away from directing for years to raise a family. Her first feature, “[Jani Be Good](https://variety.com/t/jani-be-good/),” which is playing in the [Tokyo International Film Festival](https://variety.com/t/tokyo-international-film-festival/)’s Asian Future competition, turns that experience into a portrait of four women across three generations.

“I stopped making films for over 10 years because I was having a kid and looking after my family, so getting back to it was all I really wanted,” Darmawan tells *Variety*.

Unfolding across four December days in the lead-up to Christmas, the film follows 13-year-old Jani after she overhears a fight between her 18-year-old sister Julia and their mother Winnie, and Julia leaves home. Winnie, a single mother who works as an accountant and fills fruit hamper orders on the side, grows short-tempered with the daughter who stayed. Jani, who has been secretly trading messages with Julia, leans on her grandmother, Oma, who makes spring rolls to sell so she can put money aside for her own cremation. The household is Chinese-Catholic.

### Popular on Variety

### Popular on Variety

The four leads are Chempa Puteri, Sigi Wimala, Tutie Kirana and Hyori Mika. Darmawan co-wrote the screenplay with Cyntha Hariadi. Taurisia produced for Palari Films, the Jakarta-based company she runs with fellow producer Muhammad Zaidy. Palari, founded in 2016, opens the film in Indonesian cinemas on Dec. 10.

Taurisia, an old friend, called Darmawan in 2022 with an offer to direct a family drama, a genre the filmmaker says she loves. As a working mother, she adds, family life is what she most wants to talk about right now, and only recently has she noticed how much unseen care work it demands every day. Becoming a mother, Darmawan says, also changed the way she sees her own.

“As a kid, I watched her keep the family running, rummaging through things at her desk, making phone calls, cooking dinner, but I never wondered how she felt,” she says. “It took having my own family, in my late thirties, to understand how exhausting and all-consuming it is.”

As the youngest in her own family, Darmawan grew up being treated as the one who understood least. “But that’s exactly what gave me the freedom to watch things from a distance,” she says. “You could say you can only see the constellation when you’re standing outside it.”

Jani is constantly told to be good, though she already is. The film stays with her as she slowly starts to see her mother, sister and grandmother as people with wants and failings of their own. Darmawan says people tend to assume that a household made up entirely of women will find a way to get along.

“Family problems are the same whether it’s all women or a mix of men and women, if there’s a problem in there to begin with,” she says. “Communication can break down between women too, especially because of the power dynamics in a family, where the mother, especially if she’s the breadwinner, feels she has the most right to speak the loudest.”

In many Asian families, she says, disagreements are met with silence to avoid hurting a relative. “But that ends up hurting us even more,” Darmawan says. “If it keeps getting held in and never confronted, it stays a wound and gets passed down to the next generation.”

She sees the same pattern in many all-female households, where staying quiet to avoid making a scene becomes a way of getting through the day. The film never says so outright, she adds, but it shows in how the women protect themselves at home, behind a gate that stays shut and windows fitted with bars.

Winnie responds to Julia’s departure by working harder, and her care reaches her daughters as a stream of instructions and corrections. “I didn’t want Winnie to be a villain, because she isn’t one,” Darmawan says. “I think I understand Winnie because I’m a mother too. I know how easy it is to feel like the one who has the right to speak the loudest. So I didn’t want to judge her.”

From the start, Darmawan, Hariadi and Taurisia agreed that no character would carry the blame, drawing on their own families and their experiences as daughters and mothers. The bigger creative hurdle, Darmawan says, was the co-writing itself. She had mostly written her own films before, and this time had to turn Hariadi’s prose into scenes that would hold an audience without losing the writer’s voice.

Her earlier work ran from shorts to documentaries. Her short “Sugiharti Halim” competed at Clermont-Ferrand and screened at Rotterdam and Busan, while “Silenced” also played Rotterdam. She describes those projects as small-scale, homebound and DIY, a training ground for watching quietly and letting people and spaces carry a scene.

Taurisia says she has followed Darmawan’s shorts since the early 2000s and always expected her to come back to filmmaking. What sold Palari on the project was the maturity of Darmawan’s take on womanhood and motherhood.

The production was compact. The team shot in 13 days, a first for Palari, in a house in Bandung. Darmawan, Hariadi and the four lead actors first read the script together in that house two months before cameras rolled, rehearsed in Jakarta, then returned to the location for the final two weeks of prep with cinematographer Teoh Gay Hian and production designer Suherina. None of the four actors knew each other beforehand, so the casting process included chemistry tests built around Puteri.

“I sat in on the whole process, but when it comes to the final call, I like to leave it to the director,” Taurisia says. “She’s the chef, and she knows her ingredients best.”

Palari won Locarno’s top award, the Golden Leopard, at the festival’s 74th edition with “Vengeance Is Mine, All Others Pay Cash” (Seperti Dendam, Rindu Harus Dibayar Tuntas). Its output since 2017 has ranged from “Posesif” and “Aruna and Her Palate” to Netflix original “Borderless Fog” (Kabut Berduri), “Dear David” and this year’s “Sleep No More.” For “Jani Be Good,” the company applied for international development funding without success. At home, Taurisia says, festival success brings diversity, recognition and a stronger portfolio.

“On the other hand, it can make our films look ‘too artistic’ or ‘not accessible enough,’ and local investors may see the project as risky,” she says.

The producer points to distribution as the bigger structural problem: Indonesia has exhibitors, but no distributors that reach across the archipelago. One of filmmakers’ biggest nightmares, she says, is having a film judged over a single Thursday-to-Sunday stretch before cinemas decide whether to keep it. To counter that, Palari launched Kelas Komunitas Palari (Palari Community Class) this year, a workshop series teaching film communities around the country to stage screenings and paid watch parties in their own regions. “Jani Be Good” is the program’s first test.

“Many directors struggle to make a second film after their first, and this gap in the film value chain doesn’t help,” Taurisia says. “How can we build film careers, let alone sustainable ones?”

Palari’s slate mixes returning and first-time directors. Edwin is attached to coming-of-age film “Menari dengan Bayangan” (Dancing With My Shadows, working title), a collaboration with Hindia, the solo project of singer-songwriter Baskara Putra. Aditya Ahmad’s first feature “Goldfish” picked up three awards at the Busan Asian Project Market, and Khozy Rizal’s debut feature, “I Wanna Dance With Myself,” is also on the slate.

Darmawan, who founded the independent library and bookstore Kineruku, intends to keep directing, though she expects further films to come about organically around her family and the bookshop. “As for themes, I’m open to anything, as long as it has sad and sweet relationships between people,” she says. “That’s where things get complicated and interesting.”

# West Midlands dating dealbreakers over pasta habits

![Eleanor Lawrence Profile Image](/resources/images/21237210?type=thumb)

Share

![comment icon](/resources/responsive-static/mds/images/icons/message.svg)
![]()
![](/resources/images/21644157/?type=responsive-gallery-fullscreen)
![](/resources/images/21644169/?type=responsive-gallery-fullscreen)

Share

![comment icon](/resources/responsive-static/mds/images/icons/message.svg)
![USA Today logo](/resources/responsive-static/images/usa-today-logo.svg)

Pasta habits could be a dealbreaker for nearly one in five daters in the West Midlands.

That’s according to new research from Dolmio, which found that 19 per cent of people in the region would reconsider a romantic match over a questionable approach to pasta.

The study highlights the UK’s more relaxed, and sometimes divisive, approach to Italian cuisine, with more than nine in 10 pasta eaters admitting to at least one non-traditional pasta habit.

These include swapping Italian cheese for cheddar, snapping spaghetti before cooking, and adding unconventional toppings.

Hana Hutchinson, Brand Director, Dolmio UK, said: "Pasta comes with plenty of traditions, but when it comes to our own kitchens and tables, we all have our little quirks, touches and preferences that make it our own.

![The Great British pasta debate map by Dolmio.]()The Great British pasta debate map by Dolmio. *(Image: Dolmio/Mars Food & Nutrition)*

![The Great British pasta debate map by Dolmio.]()

"Dolmio has one too: we put cream in our carbonara.

"We know pasta purists might have something to say about that, but for Dolmio, enjoying dinner isn’t about getting every rule right.

**READ MORE:** [**Birmingham’s gravy obsession revealed as diners admit unusual restaurant habit**](https://www.birmingham-now.co.uk/news/26649722.birminghams-gravy-obsession-revealed-diners-admit-unusual-restaurant-habit/?ref=ed_direct)

"Whether you snap your spaghetti, reach for cheddar or have a pasta combination that’s completely your own, we want people to enjoy meals that work for them.

"Dinner should be tasty, accessible and healthy, without worrying about getting every pasta rule right."

Nearly half of UK pasta eaters admitted to using cheddar instead of Italian cheese, while 44 per cent confessed to breaking spaghetti before cooking.

[**👉 Follow Birmingham Now's Facebook page for the latest breaking news, events, videos and stories that matter to Brummies.**](https://www.facebook.com/BirminghamNowNews?ref=ed_direct)

Thirty-eight per cent said they had mixed different pasta shapes in the same pot.

The findings are part of a broader campaign by Mars Food & Nutrition, designed to help more people enjoy fulfilling, nutritious and delicious meals.

The campaign is part of its 'Making Meals Matter' platform, which brings together its trusted brands, nutrition science, culinary expertise and partnerships to help overcome the barriers that too often stand between people and a better meal.

# $60 for a loaf of bread? New York bakery has customers lining up

## Summary

RYE by Martin Auer opened in Manhattan’s SoHo neighborhood in September and has drawn crowds for its $60 sourdough rye loaf. The bakery says the New York price reflects imported ingredients, labor and Manhattan operating expenses, while a comparable loaf costs about $16 in Austria. The attention has brought curious customers to the bakery, where the bread regularly sells out.

## Key Facts

![RYE, a popular new bakery in New York opened by Martin Auer, specializes in 100 percent rye sourdough bread. Captured from BuzzFeed Tasty's social media account](https://newsimg.koreatimes.co.kr/2026/10/31/8d27560d-a5a8-47b0-83dc-64ff9a793b26.jpg?w=728)

RYE, a popular new bakery in New York opened by Martin Auer, specializes in 100 percent rye sourdough bread. Captured from BuzzFeed Tasty's social media account

NEW YORK — Korea may have its bread pilgrimages, but Manhattan has taken the bakery craze to another level: $60 for a single loaf of rye bread.

RYE by Martin Auer, an Austrian bakery that opened in Manhattan's SoHo neighborhood in September, has quickly become one of the city's most talked-about food destinations, drawing crowds and widespread media attention for its unusually expensive sourdough rye bread.

The 1.5 kilogram loaf costs $60, but customers can also purchase half a loaf for $30 or a quarter for $15.

Located on Lafayette Street, the bakery specializes in just one type of bread. Its minimalist interior looks more like a high-end retail showroom than a traditional bakery, with customers able to watch the bread-making process.

The bread contains just three ingredients: organic rye flour, water and salt. According to the bakery, the dough undergoes a fermentation process lasting up to 24 hours, using a sourdough starter more than 50 years old.

But the price has raised eyebrows, particularly because a comparable loaf from the same bakery sells for roughly $16 in Austria.

The bakery says the higher New York price reflects the cost of importing ingredients from Austria, the labor involved in making the bread and Manhattan's high operating expenses.

The hefty price tag has sparked criticism and jokes on social media, with some questioning whether any bread is worth $60.

The attention, however, has also brought customers through the door. The bakery reported that even though they are new to the scene, the bread sells out on a regular basis, as curious New Yorkers lined up to see what made the loaf so special.

The craze may sound familiar to Koreans, where “ppangji sullye,” or bread pilgrimages, have become popular among bakery enthusiasts willing to travel long distances and wait in line for famous baked goods.

At $60 a loaf, the New York bakery is testing just how much customers are willing to pay for bread.

# Rising Again: How sourdough helped Alana rebuild her life

by

Shas­tri Boodan

When the COVID-19 pan­dem­ic brought Trinidad and To­ba­go to a stand­still, it al­so shat­tered the liveli­hood of Rio Claro res­i­dent Alana Boodoo.

The sin­gle moth­er watched her small home-based cater­ing busi­ness col­lapse al­most overnight af­ter pub­lic health reg­u­la­tions pro­hib­it­ed the sale of pre­pared foods. What had been the fam­i­ly’s pri­ma­ry source of in­come van­ished, leav­ing her strug­gling to pro­vide for her chil­dren.

Sev­er­al years lat­er, Boodoo is still re­build­ing her life.

She sur­vives on part-time jobs while rais­ing two school-aged chil­dren, but she has found a new pur­pose, and a grow­ing busi­ness, in the cen­turies-old craft of ar­ti­san sour­dough bread.

“What hap­pened dur­ing COVID forced me to start over,” Boodoo re­called. “There were days when I won­dered how I was go­ing to keep food on the ta­ble. I knew I had to learn a new skill that peo­ple would ap­pre­ci­ate.”

Boodoo’s love for cook­ing be­gan long be­fore the pan­dem­ic. She re­ceived for­mal culi­nary train­ing through cook­ing class­es of­fered by the Min­istry of Com­mu­ni­ty De­vel­op­ment, where she de­vel­oped the skills that lat­er en­abled her to op­er­ate her home-based cater­ing busi­ness. Al­though the pan­dem­ic forced that ven­ture to close, the knowl­edge she gained be­came the foun­da­tion for her lat­est en­ter­prise.

In­stead of giv­ing up, she turned back to her pas­sion for food and dis­cov­ered ar­ti­san bread-mak­ing.

To­day, the kitchen that once pro­duced catered meals is filled with the aro­ma of fresh­ly baked sour­dough loaves. Along­side bak­ing to or­der, Boodoo has start­ed teach­ing oth­ers how to make ar­ti­san bread from scratch.

“Sour­dough is more than just bread,” she said. “It’s pa­tience, sci­ence and pas­sion all work­ing to­geth­er. Every loaf tells its own sto­ry.”

Un­like or­di­nary bread made with com­mer­cial yeast, sour­dough re­lies on a liv­ing starter, a nat­u­ral­ly fer­ment­ed mix­ture of flour and wa­ter that cul­ti­vates wild yeast and ben­e­fi­cial bac­te­ria. Cre­at­ing a healthy starter can take more than a week and re­quires care­ful feed­ing and strict at­ten­tion to clean­li­ness.

“If your starter isn’t healthy, the bread sim­ply won’t rise prop­er­ly,” Boodoo ex­plained. “Many peo­ple be­come frus­trat­ed be­cause they don’t re­alise how del­i­cate the process is.”

To make the craft more ac­ces­si­ble, she plans to be­gin sell­ing ma­ture sour­dough starter cul­tures to home bak­ers.

“I want to re­move one of the biggest hur­dles for be­gin­ners,” she said. “A good starter gives you con­fi­dence and a much bet­ter chance of bak­ing a beau­ti­ful loaf.”

A labour of pa­tience

Mak­ing sour­dough is a slow, care­ful­ly timed process that usu­al­ly spans two days.

It be­gins by com­bin­ing an ac­tive starter with flour and wa­ter be­fore salt is added to form a sticky dough. In­stead of vig­or­ous knead­ing, the dough is gen­tly stretched and fold­ed sev­er­al times dur­ing the first few hours. This strength­ens the gluten while main­tain­ing the dough’s airy struc­ture.

The dough is then left to fer­ment at room tem­per­a­ture. Dur­ing this stage, the wild yeast pro­duces car­bon diox­ide while nat­u­ral­ly oc­cur­ring lac­tic acid bac­te­ria de­vel­op the dis­tinc­tive tangy flavour that sour­dough lovers cher­ish.

Once the dough has dou­bled in size, it is shaped in­to a round or oval loaf and placed in­to a proof­ing bas­ket be­fore spend­ing the night in the

re­frig­er­a­tor. The cold fer­men­ta­tion fur­ther de­vel­ops flavour, strength­ens the crumb and makes the dough eas­i­er to score be­fore bak­ing.

The fol­low­ing day, the loaf is baked in a pre­heat­ed Dutch oven or on a bak­ing stone. Steam gen­er­at­ed dur­ing the ini­tial stage of bak­ing al­lows the bread to ex­pand ful­ly, pro­duc­ing its sig­na­ture crisp, caramelised crust and soft, open in­te­ri­or. On­ly af­ter cool­ing com­plete­ly is the loaf ready to be sliced.

“It isn’t fast food,” Boodoo said with a laugh. “You can’t rush sour­dough. The bread teach­es you pa­tience, and when you cut in­to a loaf you’ve nur­tured from start to fin­ish, it’s in­cred­i­bly re­ward­ing.”

More than just bread

Be­yond its rich flavour and rus­tic ap­pear­ance, sour­dough has gained pop­u­lar­i­ty for its nu­tri­tion­al ben­e­fits.

Be­cause the dough un­der­goes nat­ur­al fer­men­ta­tion, the starch­es and pro­teins be­gin break­ing down be­fore bak­ing, mak­ing the bread eas­i­er for many peo­ple to di­gest. The lengthy fer­men­ta­tion al­so re­duces phyt­ic acid, al­low­ing the body to ab­sorb im­por­tant min­er­als such as iron, zinc and mag­ne­sium more ef­fi­cient­ly.

Stud­ies have al­so shown that sour­dough gen­er­al­ly has a low­er gly­caemic in­dex than con­ven­tion­al white bread, help­ing to slow the re­lease of sug­ar in­to the blood­stream. Tra­di­tion­al sour­dough recipes al­so con­tain on­ly a hand­ful of in­gre­di­ents, typ­i­cal­ly flour, wa­ter and salt, with­out the preser­v­a­tives com­mon­ly found in many com­mer­cial­ly pro­duced breads.

“It’s bread made the old-fash­ioned way,” Boodoo said. “Peo­ple tell me they en­joy the flavour, but many al­so say they feel fuller for longer and find it eas­i­er to di­gest.”

Be­cause every loaf is hand­craft­ed, Boodoo lim­its the num­ber of or­ders she ac­cepts each week to main­tain qual­i­ty.

“My cus­tomers un­der­stand that ar­ti­san bread isn’t mass-pro­duced,” she said. “They ap­pre­ci­ate the time, care and love that goes in­to every loaf.”

De­spite the en­cour­ag­ing re­sponse from cus­tomers, Boodoo con­tin­ues to search for sta­ble full-time em­ploy­ment. For the past two years, she has ap­plied to nu­mer­ous or­gan­i­sa­tions but has yet to se­cure per­ma­nent work.

“I’ll keep ap­ply­ing be­cause I need a steady in­come for my chil­dren,” she said. “But un­til that op­por­tu­ni­ty comes, I’ll keep bak­ing. Every loaf I sell helps pay a bill, buy gro­ceries or cov­er school ex­pens­es.”

For Boodoo, every gold­en loaf emerg­ing from her oven rep­re­sents far more than ar­ti­san bak­ing. It rep­re­sents re­silience, hope and the de­ter­mi­na­tion to rise again.

## Sourdough Cookies expand Pepperidge Farm range

![Sourdough Cookies expand Pepperidge Farm range](https://commercialbaking.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/103026-Pepperidge-Farm-Sourdough-Cookies-1024x666.png)

### Lily Cota

Lily Cota is a writer, editor and photographer from Kansas City, Missouri. She graduated from Missouri State University with a Bachelor of Science in English and a minor in Photography. When she’s not writing, you can find her reading fantasy novels, thrifting, trying out local coffee shops and spending time with her nieces.

![](https://commercialbaking.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/google-preferred-source-300x95.png)
![](https://commercialbaking.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/google-preferred-source.png)

CAMDEN, NJ — [Pepperidge Farm](https://commercialbaking.com/espresso-martini-meet-milano-cookies/) is introducing three varieties of Sourdough Cookies, made with real sourdough and specialty inclusions. These consumer-anticipated cookies are now a permanent addition to [The Campbell’s Co.](https://commercialbaking.com/campbells-recognized-among-the-civic-50-list/) portfolio.

Inspired by [increased interest in sourdough](https://commercialbaking.com/sourdoughs-reign-echoes-la-brea-bakerys-reputation/), the cookies combine modern eating trends with classic flavor profiles.

The collection includes:

**Dark Chocolate Sourdough with Brown Butter:** Dark chocolate chunks with a rich brown butter flavor.

**Cinnamon Sugar Sourdough with Vanilla Bean:** Cinnamon and crunchy pearl sugar with a hint of vanilla.

**White Chocolate Sourdough with Raspberry:** White chocolate chips with raspberry flavor.

The new cookies can be found at Walmart, with extended distribution planned for 2027. Each 8-count bag carries an SRP of $5.89.

# 8 SF Restaurants with Out-of-This-World Bread and Butter

### The term "bread and butter" is an idiom for everyday or basic fare, and diners gobble up that hunk of partially-sliced sourdough bread served with pats of foil-wrapped butter served by many classic San Francisco restaurants without giving it much thought.

At some places, though, the bread and butter is anything but basic; it’s so incredibly good, it demands your attention.

Pardon the pun, but artisanal bread has been on the rise in San Francisco since the Gold Rush, when miners and prospectors needed a way to bake bread without yeast. Our obsession with butter is more recent. According to Lisa Pike Totah, marketing director for California's leading butter producer, Challenge Dairy, per-capita butter consumption reached an all-time record high of 6.8 pounds per person in the U.S. in 2024.

"Over the past few years, butter has moved from supporting player to a hero,” she says. ”Once considered little more than a companion to toast, it now commands as much attention as the bread itself. Today's consumers are curious about flavor and often keep several different butters in their refrigerators. Chefs and restaurateurs have taken notice, offering guests a dedicated butter moment that elevates the dining experience."

A dedicated butter moment, indeed! We've had some bread and butter recently that practically made us swoon. Here are the ones that—like the best bread—made the cut.

### Outerlands

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20900%20600'%3E%3C/svg%3E) 

(Courtesy of Outerlands)

Outerlands opened in 2009, and bread and butter has been central to the restaurant since day one. The original owners worked with Chad Robertson of [Tartine](https://www.7x7.com/get-in-line-the-sf-experience-of-queuing-up-at-tartine-1787140815.html) to build out the bread program. According to executive chef Brenda Landa, the restaurant currently has a team member dedicated solely to creating boules and other bread items on the menu. They go through around 30 loaves a day.

"The starter for the sourdough here is at least as old as the restaurant itself,” says Landa. “Like many other fermented foods, the sourdough starter changes its flavor profile as it matures. Even though we're using the same starter as when we opened, that flavor has transformed, and so has the flavor of the boules."

But as good as the bread is, the butter is also a showstopper. "The butter begins with cultured creme fraiche we make in-house,” Landa continues. “We let the creme fraiche ferment for two days until it thickens before whipping it into butter. This three-day process results in a tangy butter with much more depth of flavor than your average store-bought butter."

"I can confidently say that every table dining with us orders the bread and butter," she adds. An order of pain au levain served with house-cultured butter is $10.

**Insider tip:** [Whole loaves are also available for sale](https://www.7x7.com/secret-limited-dishes-sf-restaurants-2676680137.html).

// **4001 Judah St. (Outer Sunset),** [**outerlandssf.com**](https://www.outerlandssf.com/)

### Rich Table

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20900%20600'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

# 'I Just Found Out:' Man Claims F-150 Snitches On Him To His Insurance. Ford Responds

## "They collect all your driving data," he says. But is that actually true?

![Man Buys Ford F-150. Then He Realizes It’s Snitching On Him To His Insurance](https://cdn.motor1.com/images/mgl/3WEgYA/s3/man-buys-ford-f-150.-then-he-realizes-it-s-snitching-on-him-to-his-insurance.jpg)
![Chad Swiatecki](https://cdn.motor1.com/images/static/1x1_2.gif)

***Update:** A Ford spokesperson released a statement to Motor1, saying:*

*Insurance companies have never received customer connected vehicle data from Ford without explicit consent from our customer. Before late 2024, if a customer wanted to enroll in usage-based insurance that customer had to opt in twice—first with their own insurer, then with us on their vehicle screen. Since late 2024, we haven't supported these programs at all.*

*If Ford customers suspect their insurance premiums are being raised due to their driving behavior, we recommend that they review the privacy notices and settings of non-Ford apps on their phone, as those apps may independently disclose information related to their location, speed, and other relevant data to insurance carriers.*

*Again, to be clear, insurance companies never received customer connected vehicle data from Ford without explicit consent from our customer.*

For many drivers, dealing with insurance rates can feel like an unpredictable and unwinnable battle against unseen forces who may be watching their habits throughout the day. One Ford F150 owner on Facebook claims to have discovered one of the methods used to gather data about drivers, and wants to show you how to keep your info out of their hands.

The clip from creator Matt Randolph, who goes by [Mr Global](https://www.facebook.com/reel/981883127832186) online, goes into detail about past battles some automakers have had around the issue of individual driver data collection. Randolph doesn't share how he discovered that his driving habits were being shared, but he wasn't happy about it and wanted to let others know about the methods he used to disable the data-sharing capabilities on his truck.

“They collect all your driving data, your habits and everything else, and share it with whoever, mainly your insurance company, so they can charge you more money,” Randolph said in the clip that's been viewed more than 1.3 million times. “If you have a vehicle that is or can be connected to Wi-Fi and you don't want them sharing your driver data, you might wanna check out how to turn that off.”

## Do Fords Tell On You To Your Insurance Company?

In the video, he shifts the camera toward the center screen and begins tapping through the menus in real time, narrating as he goes.

The process isn't buried behind anything that looks especially technical. A few selections in, Randolph arrives at a submenu tied to the trucks connecting features, which are the kind of place most drivers probably don't spend much time exploring after the initial setup.

That's where he pauses and points out the specific toggle that he says controls whether the vehicle shares information about how it's being driven.

After highlighting the setting, he flips it off and backs out, presenting the whole sequence as something that takes only a few seconds once you know where to look. The simplicity of it is part of what seems to catch viewers' attention since there's no special tool or workaround involved, just a setting that was already there.

For [Ford](https://www.motor1.com/news/793918/ford-f150-recall/) drivers trying to disable [driving data sharing](https://www.ford.com/support/how-tos/sync/sync-4a/how-do-i-turn-off-data-sharing-in-my-vehicle/?srsltid=AfmBOop-i50H6X_TdOHCVoWBWBvzSQPW5D5otS49MEE4-dZQxnlQTETx), the process typically involves opening the Settings menu, selecting Connectivity, navigating to Connected Vehicle Features, and switching off the Share Driving Data option.

Depending on the model year or trim, the wording and layout can vary slightly, and some features may still be tied to Connected Services or mobile apps linked to the vehicle.

What's less clear even in his own telling is how that setting [gets turned on](https://www.consumerreports.org/electronics/personal-information/how-to-stop-your-car-from-collecting-sharing-driving-data-a1233378612/#:~:text=connected%20mobile%20device.-,How%20Your%20Car%20Data%20Becomes%20a%20Treasure%20Trove,tracked%20your%20location%20and%20speed.) in the first place. At one point, he acknowledges that he may have agreed to something without realizing it.

That uncertainty hangs unanswered in the clip, opening up the possibility that the truck owner may be the one who enabled his data to be shared.

Modern vehicles often prompt drivers to [accept terms](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/03/23/how-to-stop-your-internet-connected-car-from-selling-your-driving-data.html#:~:text=What%20Ford%2C%20Hyundai%2C%20Nissan%20and,opt%20out%20of%20data%20collection.) for connected services as a sort of default during setup, and those screens can come quickly and be bundled in with everything from navigation features to remote access tools.

The question of when consent is given and how visible those choices are is already a sore spot in the industry. General Motors has faced [legal challenges](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/01/ftc-finalizes-order-settling-allegations-gm-onstar-collected-sold-geolocation-data-without-consumers) tied to the handling of driver data, part of a wave among automakers looking to collect and transmit more information than ever before. Insurers have increasingly leaned on [driving behavior data](https://www.nbcrightnow.com/national/connected-car-data-are-insurers-and-drivers-rolling-toward-dynamic-variable-pricing-insurify/article_9c90ad21-2ff2-5455-93ce-f16fdf8aaf74.html#:~:text=Usage%2Dbased%20insurance%20(UBI),behavior%2C%20not%20just%20rating%20factors.) to shape pricing models, whether through standalone apps, plug-in devices, or integrations tied directly to the vehicle.

![](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAABAAAAAJCAYAAAA7KqwyAAAAGXRFWHRTb2Z0d2FyZQBBZG9iZSBJbWFnZVJlYWR5ccllPAAAABpJREFUeNpi/P//PwMlgImBQjBqwLAwACDAAOVfAw9/ZDvcAAAAAElFTkSuQmCC)
![YouTube video player](https://cdn.motor1.com/images/video-thumbs/youtube/kFgQ-B-M0KY/s3/thumb.jpg)

## Drivers Share Their Own Data Stories

As the clip spread, the comment section quickly turned into a running debate about what that kind of data collection actually looks like in practice, and whether it works the way people think it does.

Some viewers said they’ve avoided anything that tracks their driving, convinced it will eventually be used against them. “Their way of trying to find any way to increase or cancel your insurance,” one user wrote, while another added, “I refused the drivers discount hype. I figured they would hold every single thing against me.”

Others push back, saying the trade-off can work in their favor. “I have it and the only thing that has happened is I have gotten a discount every year,” one commenter said, drawing predictable eye-rolls in reply.

The most telling responses came from people describing how the systems behave in the real world. One commenter recalled a friend flagged for extreme speeding, which was later traced to time spent flying as a helicopter nurse rather than driving. Others point to more routine frustrations: “If you drive in rush hour traffic, you'll have to brake hard at times,” one user wrote, while another said the app kept logging trips even when they weren’t behind the wheel.

*Motor1* reached out to Randolph via email and direct message.We’ll update this if he responds.

# Food tracking feels like a chore? These 7 tips make it easier

## You're not the only unenthused food tracker out there.

![](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/1b932542bf1fd247a96f923e27b9331f6930067e51eb1cbda40d069d2fdeeeaf/lightyear_networkapi/resizefit_w80_h80%3Bquality_80%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fs.yimg.com%2Fos%2Fcreatr-uploaded-images%2F2025-04%2F04fed490-1f8b-11f0-bbdb-5b8809f4dfb4)
![](https://s.yimg.com/dl/_next/static/media/googleIcon.0uvm080xk7bke.svg)

Our experts [independently review](https://shopping.yahoo.com/article/how-we-review-products-and-deals-202728651.html) everything we recommend. If you buy through our links, we may earn commission.

![Making a meal plan for several days. Concept of healthy lifestyle, sports and daily routine. Notebook, marker, dumbbells, fruit healthy food, centimetre. Diet plan. Top view, horizontal.](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/41fadf0c13cc300d9b7d1b570cdb3890c7295c8f70d0ac06fb976467b6e34e6b/lightyear_networkapi/resizefill_w976%3Bquality_80%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fd29szjachogqwa.cloudfront.net%2Fimages%2F2026-10%2Fab2610e0-8286-4112-950d-385cbd1220e1)

*Sponsored by Weight Watchers*

Food tracking sounds like a doable approach to weight loss until you're at dinner with your phone out, trying to figure out how to log a homemade stir-fry. Tracking fatigue is real. While most people are excited to dive in at first, it can end up feeling like extra homework you didn't ask for.

Experiencing food tracking fatigue doesn't mean you're doing it wrong. In fact, this is a common part of the process. "Everyone's weight loss experience is different, but tracking fatigue is one thing most people can commiserate on if it appears," Megan Bingaman, RDN, LD, nutrition lead at [Weight Watchers](https://shopping.yahoo.com/rdlw?merchantId=468ae44d-0b5e-499d-b1bf-6d656c3f9447&siteId=us-lifestyle&pageId=1p-autolink&contentUuid=42ea93d9-f422-4378-ad24-38a023e2efba&featureId=text-link&merchantName=WW+International&&signature=AQAAAY3PGQd8neayz8dOc_FbJbFcCXkIvZXd93I7lchfwrjd&gcReferrer=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.weightwatchers.com%2Fus&yMarket=us&yLocale=en-us), tells Yahoo Health. "A lot of times, we try to fit our journey into the perfect tracking system, rather than making the tracking system work for us."

Bingaman says she sees this "all the time" when meeting with members. What she's discovered: Making small changes to how you track food can cut the time and effort required without losing benefits. Ultimately, these adjustments make you more likely to stick with the process and experience the success you're working toward.

Of course, there's a difference between saying you want to tweak your approach to food tracking and actually knowing what will work for you. Here's why food tracking can become frustrating over time, plus how to make adjustments so it works for you.

## Why tracking starts to feel like a chore

Food tracking is always going to be harder than doing nothing, but there are a few key reasons it can become a source of frustration over time.

**Pressure to track perfectly.** You may feel like you need to track your intake to a T to reach your weight or health goals. "An all-or-nothing mentality is common and can contribute to or trigger tracking fatigue by introducing rigidity and perfectionism into a flexible, personalizable journey," Bingaman says.

**One missed meal snowballs … along with negative self-talk.** When you have an all-or-nothing mentality, missing a single meal can lead to negative self-talk and feelings of frustration. These can ultimately snowball, leading to further missed recordings and a cycle of negative emotions that piles up, Bingaman says. So what starts as a single missed meal becomes a missed day or missed week.

**Life stress makes tracking harder.** Life always has its ups and downs, and when things around you start to feel like a dumpster fire, tracking will naturally become more challenging. "Increased stress in other areas of life can also lead to a chore-view of tracking," Bingaman says. "That's why it is helpful to know your preferences and which tools are available to make the process simpler."

**The novelty wears off.** Almost anything new can feel fun for a little while. The problem is when the newness wears off, and you suddenly realize that food tracking is a habit you need to maintain. Consistent tracking is much harder to stay motivated with.

## Tips to make tracking easier

Having a few food tracking hacks in your back pocket can go a long way toward making the process easier for you.

### Save your repeats.

You're probably not creating new-to-you dishes at every single meal. In fact, most people cycle through the same handful of faves. For example, if you eat spaghetti, meatballs and a salad every Thursday, and you make protein pancakes for the family on Saturday mornings, make sure you save all the pertinent details in your go-to app rather than re-entering them each time.

If you're using the [Weight Watchers app](https://shopping.yahoo.com/rdlw?merchantId=468ae44d-0b5e-499d-b1bf-6d656c3f9447&siteId=us-lifestyle&pageId=1p-autolink&contentUuid=42ea93d9-f422-4378-ad24-38a023e2efba&featureId=text-link&merchantName=WW+International&&signature=AQAAAY3PGQd8neayz8dOc_FbJbFcCXkIvZXd93I7lchfwrjd&gcReferrer=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.weightwatchers.com%2Fus&yMarket=us&yLocale=en-us), you can save your favorites and simply pop them in during future tracking sessions — no additional macro-scavenging necessary. There's also a bookmark tag to simplify the process and keep all your saved foods together. This "makes tracking your go-tos just two screen taps, rather than the search-bar-and-scroll routine," says Bingaman. "Time is valuable in your journey."

### Log before you eat.

It's better — and easier — to log your meals before you dive in. "Pre-tracking your meals can eliminate memory lapses," says Bingaman. "Humans are very visual, so tracking portions and those easily-forgotten condiments is much easier when they are still in front of you." Another perk of going this route is that it can help you with real-time adjustments on details like portion sizes, giving you a way to dial in whether your dish may be higher in calories or WW points than you anticipated. "This lets you either reduce that portion size or account for [it] in your other meals and snacks later in the day," Bingaman says.

### Go "good enough" on hard days.

Some days are harder than others, and that's to be expected. "Adding guilt to those difficult days by still expecting 100% from your tracking will make the negativity worse," Bingaman says. She recommends challenging an all-or-nothing mindset by using estimates or generic insert options like "turkey sandwich" instead of feeling like you have to log every single ingredient, every time. "Tracking an estimate is still allowing you to stay consistent in a way that makes sense for you," Bingaman says.

### Use shortcuts.

Every food tracking app has its own shortcuts, so do some research to fully familiarize yourself with what your app offers. WW members can use tools like barcode scanning for quick snacks and an option to scan their plate with [AI](https://tech.yahoo.com/ai/) to track their full meal. "These tools can speed up the tracking process by removing the search and scroll from the experience," Bingaman says. "Rather than entering each thing separately, you do a quick check or edit to what it has tracked for you." She calls these great options for busy days, restaurant and holiday eating or even everyday use.

### Anchor it to a habit.

Habit stacking has become buzzy for a reason — it works. The idea is simple: You look at your routine and find a habit you're unlikely to skip, like having your morning coffee or walking your dog. Then add a habit like tracking on top of it to streamline the odds you'll pick up the new habit, Bingaman explains.

### Look back, not just down.

There will be variation in how "with it" you are in your day-to-day tracking. That's why Bingaman says it can be helpful to look at larger trends, like your weekly data, rather than focusing only on the current day. "Reviewing your tracking for the week can help you close the loop and identify what needs focus," she says. This can also help you highlight some victories outside of the number on the scale by identifying strengths from your daily eating habits that you may not notice when you're in the thick of it, says Bingaman.

### Know when to ease up.

While navigating your new habits, Bingaman says to keep an eye out for "warning signs" of tracking fatigue. These include feelings of dread, guilt or overwhelm when you sit down to log your meals. "These negative feelings harbor resentment toward what is a tool for your journey," she says. "Once you start noticing purposeful skipping of meals or a big sigh when you open the app, that's your cue to take a step back and see if there is a way to make it fit [more easily] into your lifestyle and preferences."

Ultimately, the best tracking system is one you'll keep using. "The goal of tracking is to learn about your food choices and become more intuitive with the choices you make every day, multiple times a day," Bingaman says. Your tracking system doesn't need to be perfect — it just needs to work for you. "A flawed but simplified plan you keep coming back to will help you make more progress toward your long-term goals," Bingaman says.

###### [Habit Formation](/us/basics/habit-formation)

# The Real Reason Your Habits Never Take Root

## You're not picking the wrong habit, you just quit before it took root.

Posted October 29, 2026

|
[Reviewed by Margaret Foley](/us/docs/editorial-process)

![Share on Facebook](https://cdn2.psychologytoday.com/theme-assets/icons/icon-share-round-facebook-md.svg)
![Share on X](https://cdn2.psychologytoday.com/theme-assets/icons/icon-share-round-twitter-md.svg)
![Share on Bluesky](https://cdn2.psychologytoday.com/theme-assets/icons/icon-share-round-bluesky-blue.svg)
![Share on LinkedIn](https://cdn2.psychologytoday.com/theme-assets/icons/icon-share-round-linkedin-md.svg)
![Share via Email](https://cdn2.psychologytoday.com/theme-assets/icons/icon-share-round-email-md.svg)

### Key points

Devon tried five different morning habits in one year: a tracking app, a five-minute journal, a cold-plunge routine, a [meditation](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/meditation "Psychology Today looks at meditation") app, and a paper planner. No attempt lasted more than two or three weeks before Devon decided it didn’t work. He always came to me with the same conclusion: "I tried the wrong system. I have to find the right one."

Maybe you don't own five apps. But I'd bet you've made this move before: the planner that was supposed to be the one, the workout program swapped before week three.

Every abandoned system teaches you the same lesson twice: that you're someone who starts things and doesn't finish them. And deciding to switch feels like taking action, which is the trap. Why? Because intention moves behavior far less than we assume. An analysis of 47 experiments found that a sizeable jump in what people intend to do produces only about half as large a jump in what they actually do (Webb & Sheeran, 2006).

And that’s despite the fact that the method you pick may matter less than you think it does. In a [meta-analysis](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/meta-analysis "Psychology Today looks at meta-analysis") of 52 randomized trials of [cognitive behavioral](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/cognitive-behavioral-therapy "Psychology Today looks at cognitive behavioral") [therapy](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/therapy "Psychology Today looks at therapy") for [addiction](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/addiction "Psychology Today looks at addiction"), CBT beat usual or minimal care but was no better than any other evidence-based treatment (Magill et al., 2026). That matches what I see in my work: When it comes to good-enough options, staying matters more than choosing.

## Making a Plan Makes the Practice Stick

Researchers at UC Berkeley (Susman et al., 2026) recruited 497 adults and taught them the same practice: a private, comforting hand-over-heart gesture, held for 20 seconds. Everyone chose a cue ("when I finish brushing my teeth, I'll do it").

Then they split the groups: Half stopped there, while the other half watched a 15-minute video on habit science and filled out a written plan. They pre-decided when they'd practice, where, what might get in the way, and the payoff the practice would give them. They set a daily phone reminder, got permission for two "skip days" a week, and closed by visualizing the plan.

What did they find? Six months later, the second group practiced more often and more automatically. They also reported more self-compassion and fewer mental health symptoms. Gains in automaticity over the first three months accounted for roughly 40 percent to 83 percent of those six-month differences. The effects were small, but real: about two extra practice sessions a week, roughly a third more practice than the cue-only group.

Importantly, the trial tested the whole package, so it can't say which piece did the work. But I believe that simply setting a vision of who you'll become gives you a future self to measure against, and you come up short of that every single day. But a plan gives you a planned program of repetitions to measure against, and you can hit that today (and tomorrow, until you match that future vision).

You're not weak-willed. You just haven't put in enough reps, in the same place and at the same time, for anything to take root. The "21 days to a habit" figure has no evidence behind it. In one study, new habits took anywhere from 18 to 254 days to become automatic (Lally et al., 2010), roughly three weeks to eight months. Have you given your new habits that much time?

The same thing plays out in many "tried and failed" efforts: the Sunday call to your mother, the workout program restarted every January. Each new start feels difficult before it roots, and you read that difficulty as proof you can't do it, or that you planted the wrong seed. By the fifth time, you start to suspect the problem is you. Devon wasn't really trying a sixth system; he was unsure whether habits even work for him.

## Why You Keep Quitting Before It Sticks

So why do smart, motivated people keep switching too early? Here’s what I’ve seen with clients:

**Starting feels like doing something.** Week one pays off quickly: it's new (releases [dopamine](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/dopamine "Psychology Today looks at dopamine")), gives a sense of progress, and may even get noticed by others. If enthusiasm got noticed growing up and follow-through didn't, that pull runs even stronger. Nobody claps for week six of the same [boring](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/boredom "Psychology Today looks at boring") routine.

![](https://cdn2.psychologytoday.com/assets/styles/manual_crop_1_1_75x75/public/teaser_image/blog_entry/2026-10/breaking_habits.jpg?h=2d486e54&itok=WxM1kvlp "Lidiia Moor | iStock")
![](https://cdn2.psychologytoday.com/assets/styles/manual_crop_1_1_75x75/public/teaser_image/blog_entry/2026-08/pexels-kuiyibo-13993722.jpg?h=ebe0b791&itok=JRxCgb1e "Kuiyibo Campos / Pexels")

**Comparing options feels responsible.** Spending time researching the "right" recovery framework can feel like proof that you care. Many of us were taught, in school or by an achievement-minded parent, that a "right" answer is out there waiting, and researching reads as diligence. But it's [procrastination](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/procrastination "Psychology Today looks at procrastination") research—aim, aim, aim, but never fire.

**The stretch before something roots feels hardest, and that's when you bail.** The cost usually shows up well before the payoff. A fruit tree may bear no fruit for two to three years... that's not a sign it won't. If an early setback got treated as proof something was broken when you were younger, that reading is probably still running. You have to learn to sit with the strain and keep going.

Any of those sound familiar?

## When Switching Is the Right Call

Does all this mean you should never switch? Not at all. If a practice is making things worse, stop. If a 6 a.m. journal can't survive your night shifts, the fit is the problem. And early on, trying a few options is a reasonable search.

The trick is to switch on purpose. Set a stopping rule *before* you start: how many weeks you'll give it, and how you'll track success. Then count repetitions, and track whether it's getting easier and moving you toward your goal. If you're just working and nothing is getting better, it may be time to switch. Handled that way, you can make a switch with data, instead of only because it's hard.

## How to Write the Plan

A cue tells you when to start, but not where, what might stop you, or why you're bothering. Put all four in one sentence: "At 7 a.m., after coffee, in the kitchen, I will write down three things I'm [grateful](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/gratitude "Psychology Today looks at grateful") for in my journal; if the baby's up early, I'll do it on my phone in the baby's room, because noticing the good in my life makes me a better father."

Name the reward and set the reminder before you need either. Decide while you're calm. In my experience, the tired and [stressed](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/stress "Psychology Today looks at stressed") moments usually win, and you fall back on what's familiar.

Decide what a skip day means before you miss one. An undefined miss can feel like failure, and a broken streak is probably an excuse you've used to start over before. Give yourself two skips a week. Script for the day you miss: "That's one of my two. Tomorrow I'm back on."

## Remember This

In simple terms: Give the habit in front of you a full plan, a fair number of weeks, and a way to see whether it's working. The strain in week two is the friction growth requires; your tracking tells you whether this habit is worth it. I've done plenty of switching myself. We're all human, after all.

What's the one habit you'd write the whole plan for this week?

*If this pattern sounds familiar, my book* [Unhooked](https://readunhooked.com) *goes deeper into what makes change durable. A fuller evidence review of why [willpower](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/self-control "Psychology Today looks at willpower") isn't the mechanism lives* [*here*](https://adijaffe.com/atlas/behavior-change/why-does-willpower-fail)*.*

References

Webb, T. L., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Does changing behavioral intentions engender behavior change? A meta-analysis of the experimental evidence. *Psychological Bulletin, 132*(2), 249-268. <https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.132.2.249>

Magill, M., Nichols, L. M., Kiluk, B. D., Alton, E., Tartak, O., & Ray, L. A. (2026). A meta-analysis of cognitive behavioral therapy for substance use disorder: Treatment effects by comparator type and consumption and psychosocial outcomes. *Behaviour Research and Therapy, 203*, 105101. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.brat.2026.105101>

# Greg Schwem: If you wish to attend my funeral, save the date!

![Greg Schwem](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAQAAAADCAQAAAAe/WZNAAAAEElEQVR42mM8U88ABowYDABAxQPltt5zqAAAAABJRU5ErkJggg==)

Greg Schwem

I’ve never considered myself a procrastinator, but I’ve decided it’s time to tackle all those household projects I’ve recently been avoiding.

After all, Aug. 14, 2046, will be here before I know it.

That is the date I will leave this earth. At least according to Death Clock: The Life Lab, the morbidly named “health and wellness” app that predicts when users will meet their demise. As Halloween approaches, what better time to learn about one’s own mortality?

Launched in 2024 by entrepreneur Brent Franson, the app encourages users to make lifestyle changes that could add years to their lives. That could mean eating more broccoli or getting a simple blood test. The latter is included with a paid subscription of $69.99 annually or $14.99 per month.

Death Clock, Franson said, morphed from a mental health app idea he dubbed “Most Days.” Franson, who struggled with marijuana and alcohol addiction in earlier years, likened Most Days to a habit tracking intake form used by mental health facilities. Silicon Valley investors were interested but, he admits, not overwhelmed with enthusiasm.

Seeing a likely death date on one’s phone seemed more engaging, Franson said, although the concept was originally called Most Days. Death Clock was more of a tongue-in-cheek title employees used around the office. The Death Clock staff is small — around six employees — but also contains a board featuring clinical physicians and chaired by an oncologist from the Stanford School of Medicine. Eventually, Franson said, the new name stuck.

More than 1.5 million users have downloaded Death Clock. Upon sign-up, they discover their life expectancies via a series of questions on subjects ranging from daily vegetable intake to water consumption to social habits and marital status. I am recently divorced and not sure if that information contributed to my death date. I do know it would play a role if the app were called “Financial Death Clock.”

The AI-driven app then crunches that data with numbers derived from longevity studies and life expectancy tables. Eventually the app spits out an expected death day and calendar year. My day was accompanied by a graphic featuring a skeleton floating in a pool on what appeared to be a sprinkled donut.

“We’re trying to lighten it up,” Franson said.

The user also has the option to create a “save the date” message featuring, in my case, a simple, “Greg is going to die Tuesday, Aug 14th, 2046 at age 84.”

With the exception of my 90-year-old mother, I have already forwarded this information to my friends and relatives in hopes they can clear their schedules. For the record, I have already left instructions in my will for what I KNOW is going to be a rockin’ Celebration of Life party.

I’m fine with a life expectancy of 84, even though Death Clock says I could reach 90 if I made a few lifestyle changes. At least Death Clock didn’t tell me I was going to die in the coming months. Franson said a prediction like that is highly unlikely.

“It’s only predicting based on preventable health,” he said. “it’s not like an astrologist that’s going to say, ‘Hey, I think you’re going to get hit by a bus next week.’”

Considering I just renewed my city bus pass, that’s a relief. But knowing I only have 20 remaining years has caused me to rethink a few impending decisions. Purchasing “lifetime warranties” from Amazon no longer seems like a good idea. Ditto for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage. Then there’s the dilemma about when to take Social Security.

But I suppose an extra year or two wouldn’t hurt me. I’m headed to the grocery store today and plan to throw some extra vegetables and bottled water into my cart.

Who knows? There might be a concert I wish to see in 2047.

*(Greg Schwem is a veteran comedian, motivational speaker and humor specialist known for blending business insights with standup comedy. He is also the author of three Amazon bestsellers. His latest, “Turning Gut Punches into Punch Lines: A Comedian’s Journey Through Cancer, Divorce and Other Hilarious Stuff,” was released in September 2024. Visit Greg on the web at [www.gregschwem.com](http://www.gregschwem.com).)*

# **Samsung Health Offers Free AI Training to Prevent Diabetes in the Elderly**

28 Oktober 2026, 10:05 |   [Editorial Team](#) 

* ![](https://imgsrv2.voi.id/ihOZcHyvK42wL1PVj_zLO5qANDooQYUmnqlJYTEhRks/auto/30/30/sm/1/bG9jYWw6Ly8vdXNlcnMvRGVjZW1iZXIyMDIyL0kzS0xUZzJGWW9JMkZyT0FhZVY2LmpwZWc.jpg)

* ![](https://imgsrv2.voi.id/ihOZcHyvK42wL1PVj_zLO5qANDooQYUmnqlJYTEhRks/auto/30/30/sm/1/bG9jYWw6Ly8vdXNlcnMvRGVjZW1iZXIyMDIyL0kzS0xUZzJGWW9JMkZyT0FhZVY2LmpwZWc.jpg)

  [Ary Julianto](https://voi.id/en/artikel/tim-redaksi/84/editor) Editor

![Samsung Health Offers Free AI Training to Prevent Diabetes in the Elderly](https://imgsrv2.voi.id/erIEuSX9o0fvl4DJxiJbIZOwrVbzNpMBVlaoooUdAR8/auto/1200/675/sm/1/bG9jYWw6Ly8vcHVibGlzaGVycy82MDAyODkvMjAyNjEwMjcxOTU2LW1haW4uY3JvcHBlZF8xNzkzMTA1Nzc0LmpwZw.jpg) 

Samsung Health collaborates with Lark Health to provide free AI training for the elderly (photo: x @smasithick ·)

Share:

[![twitter](https://asset.voi.id/images/partials/twitter-white.png)](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?source=https://voi.id/en/technology/600289&text=Samsung Health Offers Free AI Training to Prevent Diabetes in the Elderly https://voi.id/en/technology/600289 "twitter")      [![feedly](https://asset.voi.id/images/partials/FD.png)](https://feedly.com/i/subscription/feed%2Fhttps%3A%2F%2Fvoi.id%2Frss%2F "feedly")

JAKARTA - Samsung Health has teamed up with digital health platform Lark Health to bring an artificial intelligence (AI) based health support service for people aged 65 and over. This program is designed to help the elderly prevent type 2 diabetes and manage the risk of chronic diseases through digital support that is available around the clock.

Samsung Electronics America announced the partnership by integrating the Lark Health diabetes prevention and health support program into the Samsung Health app. Users who meet the requirements can obtain AI training services, monitoring daily habits, and access to clinical resources at no cost to be paid for themselves.

One of the services available is the Medicare Diabetes Prevention Program. Participants aged 65 and over who meet the requirements can participate in the program to receive 24-hour AI-based support, personal habit tracking, and access to clinical resources. They can also use connected health devices, including smart scales with mobile connectivity, at no additional cost to their own pockets.

For seniors who do not meet the strict requirements of Medicare, Samsung provides an alternative in the form of a one-year free Lark Prevention program. The service is usually priced at 249 US dollars or around Rp4.51 million, based on the exchange rate of Rp18,100 per US dollar.

The Lark Prevention program was developed in collaboration with behavioral change scientists from Harvard and Stanford. Its accompanying materials include practical guides on diet, sleep, stress management, and physical activity to help users build healthier living habits.

According to the information conveyed in the announcement, more than two million patients have used Lark's interactive lessons to implement healthier lifestyle choices in their daily lives.

This initiative is the first step in a broader plan to expand long-term health support through the US federal government's ACCESS model. In future updates, the digital support service is planned to include cardiometabolic health and behavioral well-being, while maintaining clinical professional supervision.

Lark Health President, Julia Hu, said partnerships with widely used mobile platforms can help reach more elderly people through devices they already use every day.

This program also expands Samsung's efforts to develop digital health services. Samsung Health has previously been accepted in the Medicare App Library directory. The company is also running the Kill the Clipboard initiative to reduce the use of physical documents in administrative processes in doctor's offices.

Through integration with Lark Health, Samsung is expanding the functions of Samsung Health from a health monitoring application to a digital support tool for chronic disease prevention. The availability of a free program for users who meet the requirements provides additional options for the elderly to monitor health habits and obtain guidance in leading a healthier lifestyle.
